meta.tagline: How could the son of a noble Brahmin give up everything to row a ferry for the rest of his life?

1.text: Book One · Leaving Home to Seek the Way

I have poled a boat on this river all my life. Among my passengers there are often those who recognise me as of Brahmin birth, and they ask me: how does the son of the noblest Brahmins come to pole a boat on a river?
To answer truly, I must begin from a night very far away.

That night I was only in my teens. In front of my father's house I stood the whole night through, arms folded on my chest, like a statue.
For I had made up my mind to cast everything aside, to leave home and follow the Samanas—poor, ragged, naked, filthy, practising austerities like outcasts. My father, naturally, would not allow it, and so I stood at his door all night begging him.
When the moon rose, he got up and looked at me once; when the moon set, he looked at me again.

At daybreak he laid his hand on my shoulder and said: Go, into the woods. If you find the joy of heaven, come back and teach me; if you meet disillusion, come back to my side as well.
Then I thought I knew what it was I was looking for.

I dragged my stiffened legs out of the still-sleeping town. From the last little house at the edge of the town a man slipped out and joined me—Govinda, the friend who grew up with me under the same banyan tree.
He said that wherever I went, he would go; he would follow me and be my shadow. But in the end he too left me.
Why did two who grew up together, inseparable, later part ways and take two different roads?

2.text: Book Two · Samsara of the World

I left that grove alone. Govinda, my most faithful friend, had left me too. As I walked out of the woods I found that I had left behind my teachers, my friend, and the road I had always walked, yet my heart was light and bright. For the first time in three years I felt hunger, and for the first time felt hunger to be a good thing: to heed the voice and the craving within oneself is the first step toward perceiving the self.

That evening I came to a great river. The water was wide, with endless woods on both banks, and dusk spread over the surface bit by bit. On the shore stood a hut, and the ferryman was drawing in his oar. I asked him to let me lodge for the night and take me across the next day. He looked over my Samana garb and asked where I was going. For a moment I had no answer.

Once I was a noble Brahmin, then a Samana in the woods, and now I am merely Siddhartha, awakened—I am no one. Not a craftsman, who might belong to a guild and find a place to live in it; not an ascetic, who might practise with the Samanas; for the first time I belonged to no group. Where should I belong? Whose life should I join?

Beyond the river lay a city, prosperous and extravagant. In that city I would live twenty years, learning to write, to keep accounts, to drink, and to love; with a house, servants, and a room of fine clothes, I gave myself to feeling the human world's self. But one morning many years later, I, who had money, friends, and a lover, once again cast everything aside, left again, and walked toward the river, not knowing where it ended. What had those twenty years of wealth and splendour given me? And what made me give it all up?

3.text: Book Three · The River Made Whole

That day I came to the river wanting to die. On the water I saw my own face, old, slack, ruined by wine and dice, and I leaned my body out over the river. Just then I heard a voice in the water. Only one word, low and steady. I drew my body back and fell asleep among the roots of a tree.

When I woke, a monk was keeping watch beside me, afraid a snake would bite me as I slept by the river. He did not know me; I knew him—Govinda, my dear friend of youth. He was still looking for his own road, and had looked all his life. He asked who I was and where I was going. I said, I am on a pilgrimage. After he left I sat a long time. I did not want to go back to the city, and did not want to go into the woods again.

I thought of the ferryman who had carried me across twenty years before. He could not read; he could only pole a boat, braid rope, mend oars, but he said the river could speak, only I could not hear it then. I walked along the bank, a whole day long. At dusk the river rose; the ferry was still there, the hut was still there, the ferryman was still there, only his hair had turned entirely white.

He asked me aboard, the long oar dipped, and we left the bank. I gazed at the water, and suddenly envied beyond measure this life he lived in the river's company. Afterwards I settled by this river and learned to pole. Why did that stay become a whole life? What did the river say to me at last? And which old friend would I meet again, to stir me so deeply, and so sadly?

segments.text: The ferryman Vasudeva put the oar into his hands, walked into the woods, and did not come back. He kept the ferry alone, and carried people across. Some went to market, some to a funeral, some only to look once upon a daughter; the river and he listened in silence, and never asked more.
Many years passed. An old friend with white hair, Govinda, came to the ferry. He had sought all his life and was still seeking his own road, and once again he did not recognise the man at the pole.

Siddhartha bade him look down at the water. Upon it rose a thousand thousand faces: child, old man, fish, the dying, the newborn, flowing away together and flowing back together. The old friend kissed his brow. Tears fell on the boards of the boat, and he himself could not say why.

This work is adapted from Siddhartha, the classic novel by Nobel laureate Hermann Hesse. Many say that the novel is too obscure and hard to follow, or holds so much philosophical speculation that they cannot read on.

Though there are many interpretations, to my eyes this classic novel never clings to conveying some particular doctrine; instead it lets different people read different insights from it, insights tied only to each person's own experience. In my eyes, Siddhartha is really about the whole of one person's life.
In youth we chase lofty beliefs, thirst for truth, seek the self, always thinking the answer lies hidden in the road ahead;
In early manhood we must fall into the world, swept along by desire, wealth, and vanity, chasing wants and tasting every gain and loss;
In old age we turn suddenly to face decay, strip away the show, and all at once everything outward grows tasteless, and we savour the sourness;
Perhaps we are given happiness and hope anew through our children, wishing to command them, wishing our love to be repaid; but in the end no one can command another young life.

This work is heavy with text, yet I have tried to condense and summarise the original story as far as I could, hoping that through the form of a text game it may help everyone read a classic more easily.

Cello and bansuri bamboo flute play the River motif: a five-note pentatonic phrase that rises and falls like water together in tender counterpoint, tanpura drone and soft river, a gentle harmonium chord at the end like a bow to the ground. Recognition, tears, love; nothing left to seek. Simple, warm, deeply resolved final cadence. 2-3 minutes.

e_xidaduo.name: Siddhartha
e_xidaduo.desc: The one this story follows. Son of a Brahmin noble of ancient India, handsome and keen of mind, he left home to seek peace of the heart, and his life rose and fell more than once.

fields.label: Birth
fields.text: The highest caste of ancient India—the Brahmin, hereditary priestly nobles who kept the sacrifices and the recitation of scripture

fields.label: Name in youth
fields.text: He could recite every scripture, and at sacrifice he served beside his father; the elders said he would be a priest among priests

fields.label: Disquiet
fields.text: He had everything and could not be glad: he doubted that bathing, sacrifice, and scripture could give the heart true peace

fields.label: How he left home
fields.text: He made no quarrel; he only stood a night before his father's door. At daybreak the father yielded, and he said no further farewell

archive.title: A rich man of the city

fields.label: Livelihood
fields.text: He learned trade from the richest merchant of the great city, yet treated gain and loss as a game

fields.label: Three arts
fields.text: Thinking, waiting, fasting—the three treasures he carried into the city from his years as a Samana

fields.label: Possessions
fields.text: A house, servants, a room of fine clothes, and beyond the city a garden of mango trees

fields.label: Sickness of the heart
fields.text: The richer he grew, the more he feared losing, age, and death; at night he dreamed of money, and waking to the mirror found a stranger's face

fields.label: New station
fields.text: Apprentice to the ferryman: poling, tilling, weaving baskets, learning from the river how to listen

fields.label: The old arts
fields.text: Thinking, waiting, fasting—only one still served: patiently waiting for a child who would not own him

fields.label: The wound
fields.text: The day the son fled, he pursued as far as the garden gate at the city's edge, stood a long time, and at last knew he could not bring him back

fields.label: Journey's end
fields.text: Among the river's thousand voices he heard at last the sound of perfection, and was reconciled with the whole world

e_qiaowenda.name: Govinda

fields.label: That night
fields.text: He pressed forward to ask for a place, without waiting for his friend to speak first—the first step he ever took alone

fields.label: Parting

fields.label: As he is now
fields.text: White-haired, he still wanders; he has sought a lifetime and still feels he has found nothing

fields.label: The old habit
fields.text: He asks his old friend, “Show me a path,” and for decades has followed him, still searching for his own

fields.label: The last scene
fields.text: He bent and kissed his old friend's brow. Tears fell on the boards of the boat, and he himself could not say why

e_qiaodamo.name: Gotama
e_qiaodamo.desc: The Buddha, the Blessed One, called Shakyamuni in later ages. The awakened one of legend; he taught in the Jetavana monastery at Savathi, and his disciples were many upon the earth.

fields.text: Men call him the Buddha, “the one who has awakened”; disciples and the faithful honour him as the Blessed One

fields.label: Bearing
fields.text: His walking, the fall of his hands, the lowering of his gaze, all showed perfection; by that peace alone he could be known among hundreds of monks

fields.label: What he taught
fields.text: Four things: suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path—life is suffering; suffering has a source; the source can be quenched; there is a way to quench it

fields.label: Later years
fields.text: Old as he was, he still walked from place to place to teach; the world began to say his time among men was short

fields.label: What he left
fields.text: He left no wonders, but a path anyone might walk, and a company still walking it

fields.label: The eye that sees

fields.label: In her heart
fields.text: She herself admitted she did not know how to love; those who can love are ordinary people, and that is their secret

fields.label: The loved thing in the cage
Later years
fields.text: She closed the garden gate, dismissed her guests, gave the garden beyond the city to the order, and set out with her son

fields.label: The one she went to see
Cause of death
fields.text: A black snake in the grass by the road bit her; she reached the ferry and could not rise again

fields.label: Last words
fields.text: She said she had meant to look once upon that holy one, and had found only the lover of former days, and that this too was well

e_weisudewa.name: Vasudeva
e_weisudewa.desc: Ferryman at the crossing in the woods. An ordinary man who could not read, yet he knew best the art of listening—he had learned everything from the river.

fields.label: Appearance
fields.text: An ageing ferryman, his face lined with fine smiling wrinkles, few of speech; when he smiled his eyes shone

fields.label: How he received guests
fields.text: He would share bread, water, and mangoes with a traveller who had nothing, and did not press for the ferry-fee

fields.label: A strange saying
fields.text: He said the river had taught him: water flows out and returns; who ferries a man today will be repaid in time

fields.label: Art
fields.text: To carry men across, and to hear them speak; among a thousand travellers, only four or five could hear the river talking

fields.label: Unlettered

fields.label: The dead wife
fields.text: His wife had died of illness many years before, and was burned on the mound beside the ferry; thereafter he kept the river alone

fields.label: What taught him
fields.text: His teacher was the river: it taught him to listen, and that time does not exist in the world

fields.label: What he passed on at parting
How he taught
fields.text: He never spoke doctrine; he only brought a man to the water and sat with him—what is told no one hears; what is tasted for oneself is experience

fields.label: Farewell
fields.text: When his friend had heard the sound of perfection, he walked into the woods and into the oneness of all things

cards.title: Son of a Brahmin

segments.text: [[NPC1]] had a high brow and a look like a king's. He grew up playing amid his mother's songs, and at his father's side on the riverbank learned the pious bath—the daily rite by which Brahmin nobles pray to be washed of sin; early he joined the talk of scholars and argued the {{e_feituo|Vedas}}—the sacred scriptures handed down among the Brahmins, source of sacrifice and wisdom.
At every rite his bearing was perfect and graceful; at every debate his speech was keener than other men's. Strong and handsome, quick and clever, the most elegant prince could be no more.

In ancient India, two thousand five hundred years ago, people divided society into several ranks called “castes,” fixed from birth for a lifetime. Highest of them was the {{e_poluomen|Brahmin}}—hereditary priestly nobles who presided over sacrifice and recited the scriptures, who held themselves nearest the gods and were honoured by all, even kings. He was the perfect son born into just such a Brahmin house, and grew up in a mansion planted with mango trees, where the scent of the sacrificial fire hung all year.

Everyone around him loved him. Young women of the town felt a ripple in their hearts when they saw him; his friend {{e_qiaowenda|Govinda}}, himself the son of a Brahmin noble, revered him above anyone else. His love for [[NPC1]] was not merely of the surface: he loved his words and deeds, his wisdom, his lofty and ardent thoughts, and was even willing to be his shadow, following wherever he went. From boyhood Govinda had followed him wholeheartedly, as one follows a faith.

[[NPC1]] could make everyone glad—yet he himself was not glad. When the smoke of sacrifice rose, bewilderment and unrest rose with it; from the glittering stars of night, from the flowing river, unquiet thoughts came upon him without cease. Whatever others expected of him, he could do. But why did his own heart so often feel parched, unable to find what it truly longed to seek? A seed of unrest had long been buried quietly in his heart.

{{e_fuqin|Father}} was the town's most honoured priest, in white robe and sacred thread, his bearing calm and noble. He poured all his heart into this son, and, filled with joy as he looked at him, said to whoever would hear—
My son is keen of mind, and hungry for knowledge. One day he will be a great scholar, a priest, a prince among Brahmins. My whole life will shine because of him.

As he said this, the father's eyes were full of hope. His mother, watching him greet her, would always lift her chest with pride; the teachers kept their finest verses for him, hoping he would soon take the key of the sacrificial fire. But none of them knew his unhappiness. In his gaze upon the fire there was no contentment, only a thirst that deepened day by day. Neither the glory of this house nor the future all men envied could hold a heart already stirring to leave.

cards.title: The Vessel Unfilled

segments.text: My father and my teachers have been very kind to me. They poured their finest wisdom, drop by drop, into the vessel of my body, as one pours water into a jar. In the scripture hall of the {{e_poluomenzhai|Brahmin house}}, I read the {{e_feituo|Vedas}}—the sacred scriptures our Brahmins have handed down from age to age—volume after volume, and debated scholar after scholar. Yet my vessel was never filled, my heart was not satisfied, my soul was not at peace.

Pious bathing is a good thing, yet it is only water—it can wash the dust from the body, not the unrest from the heart. The rites of offering to the gods are very beautiful; but is that all there is? Why must my father, who has done no wrong, bathe himself anew each day, trying to wash his sins away? Why do even the most learned elders have hunger written in their eyes? Does the spring not lie within a man himself? To whom else should one offer sacrifice, whom else revere, if not to that?
I still have too many questions, and no one to tell them to, no one who could understand; even I myself have never understood what it is I am truly seeking.

The scriptures say that in the depths of every person there is an undying “true Self,” called {{e_atman|Atman}}, one with the spirit of the universe. The wise know everything of the world—creation, speech, food, the stars—but if they do not know this one thing that matters, of what use is all that knowledge?

I must find the spring within myself. A man must possess it—everything else is only detour and error. No one can point this path for me: not my father, not my teachers, not the sacred verses. This is my care, my thirst, my sorrow.

cards.title: I Will Follow You

segments.text: Evening, under the {{e_rongshu|banyan outside town}}, two youths had just risen from meditation. By day three {{e_shamen|Samana}} had passed through the city—ascetics who had left their homes to wander, almost naked, their shoulders thick with dust and blood, like the destitute outcasts of the world. Strangely, though, there was about them a resolute stillness, a harsh holding to the self—had they already grasped the Self? [[NPC2]] had just silently recited the sacred syllable {{e_om|Om}}—the ancients said: Om is the bow, the heart the arrow, and the target of the arrow is Brahman. In that moment the arrow in his own heart had left the string.
Friend, tomorrow morning I shall join the Samanas and become an ascetic.
What are you saying? Samanas? Those naked, gaunt, filthy men who passed through the city today?
Just so. They have nothing, and yet they seem to lack nothing. I want to practise as they do—to peel desire away layer by layer, and see what is left at the last.
But… but will your father allow it? You are the son he is proudest of, the most promising young man in the whole city! And in time you are to—
We need not waste words. At dawn tomorrow I begin the life of a Samana. Let us speak of it no more.
Why? Tell me why! Learning, fame, the love of the teachers—things other men cannot obtain though they beg for them—you have them all. What else is there to seek?

Peace. Sacrifice, scripture, debate—I have tried them all, and the thirst in my heart grows deeper day by day. The vessel of my body is full of water, yet my heart has always been empty. Better to go into hardship than to wither here slowly—either I find that spring, or I die upon the road that seeks it.
Then will you come back?
I do not know. Perhaps I will return if I find it; perhaps I will be on the road all my life.
You will take no dry provisions? Not even a garment against the cold?
A Samana wants nothing. Sleep, my friend. When the sun rises tomorrow, do not see me off.

At dawn the next day, [[NPC2]] left the still-sleeping town alone. At the last hut on the edge of the city, a crouched figure slipped from the shadows and silently followed him. The night before, when that announcement was first heard, this face had gone pale as a dried banana skin.
I have come. Do not send me back. I have made up my mind: wherever you go, I will follow—as your companion, as your servant, as your shadow.
You came after all.
I did not sleep all night. I have decided: your path is my path. If you are to become a saint, I will watch you become one.
Fool. Each man has his own path; no one can walk another's. Still—come.

cards.title: Standing Until Dawn

segments.text: The night grew deep. [[NPC1]] entered the room of the most honoured old priest in the house and stood silently behind him. He had come to ask a tremendous thing: to leave home and become a {{e_shamen|Samana}}—a wandering ascetic who forsakes his family and goes naked into hardship. The old man felt the presence at his back.
Is it you? My son, speak your mind.
With your leave, I have come to tell you: I wish to leave your house tomorrow, to join the ranks of the ascetics and become a Samana. I am certain you will not oppose it.

The old man was silent a long while. In the night sky beyond the little window the stars moved without a sound. The son stood with his arms crossed upon his breast, motionless; the old man sat motionless upon the mat. At last the old man spoke—
It would be unseemly for us to speak in violent and angry words. Yet there is displeasure in my heart. I do not wish to hear you make such a request again.
Why do you still wait?
You know why.

The old man walked away in vexation and returned to his bed. An hour passed; he could not sleep. He rose and paced, and through the little window he saw the young man standing with folded arms, his pale robe faintly gleaming in the dark. Another hour passed; the moon climbed the sky. He rose again and saw the moonlight like water upon the young man's bare ankles. His heart filled with anger and anxiety, with fear and grief—the one he had raised for half a lifetime was defying him in a way he had never imagined, never seen.
In the last hour before dawn the old man came out once more. The young man still stood there, tall and strange.
Why do you wait?
You know why.
Will you stand like this until dawn, until noon, until night?
If you do not consent, I shall stand and wait.
You will grow tired.
I will not grow tired.
You will fall asleep.
I will not fall asleep.
You will die.
I will not die.
Then you would rather die than obey me?
I have always obeyed you.
Then will you give up your intention?
I will do what you require of me, but in my heart I am unwilling to give up my intention.

The first light of day fell upon them. The old man saw the young man's knees tremble a little—yet there was no weariness in his face, and his gaze rested firmly on the distance. At last the old man understood: this son could no longer remain in the house; he had already left. He stretched out his hand and laid it gently on the young man's shoulder.

Good. Go, then, into the forest, and be a Samana. If you find the bliss of heaven in the woods, come back and teach it to me; if you meet with disillusion, return to me still, and together we shall offer sacrifice and penance to the gods. Now go and kiss your mother farewell, and tell her where you are going.

With that, the old man's hand slid from the young man's shoulder. He turned and went out toward the {{e_muyuhepan|river bathing place}}—the stone steps on the riverbank at the city's edge, where he bathed each morning, praying to wash his sins away. But today he walked more slowly than ever before. In the room the young man tried to take a step; his body swayed—he had stood in that one place the whole night through.

cards.title: I Will Not Tire

segments.text: My knees are trembling; I can feel it. I have stood half the night; my legs no longer seem my own. Starlight lies on my shoulders, and dew has made the robe ice-cold. But my heart does not tremble. Three times my father came from the little window to look at me, each time thinking I would sit down, would give in. I will not. I listen to his footsteps as he goes back inside, heavier each time.

I am not defying him. There is no son under heaven who would wish his beloved father to rise three times in a night, sleepless. But if I give back half a step now, I must stay, and walk the road he has laid for me—to become a {{e_poluomen|Brahmin}}. Through the highest caste of ancient India, to become one of the hereditary priestly nobility: honourable, dignified, respected by all.

And then? A lifetime of sacrifice, bathing, reciting scripture—and another lifetime of thirst. He has everything—learning, virtue, fame—but has he ever been content? Each day he bathes, trying to wash away an unrest that will not wash; each day he offers sacrifice, trying to reach a heaven he cannot reach—I have watched it all with my own eyes. I will not become another him: learned, respectable, but never satisfied.

The scriptures say there is in a man's heart an undying “true Self,” called {{e_atman|Atman}}, one with the spirit of the universe. It is not in the smoke of the sacrificial fire, nor in the letters of a prayer, but only in the depths of a man himself. Perhaps only by finding it will one gain true contentment of heart. I will go and find it, even if it takes a lifetime.
Dawn is near; the stars are fading one by one. Legs, you may tremble; heart, you may not. I will stand until dawn, until noon, until night—until he himself gives me leave to go.

cards.title: Eagle and Jackal

segments.text: The years in the forest were counted in hunger. [[NPC1]] took one meal a day, and never cooked it; then he tried fasting fourteen days, and once again twenty-eight. The {{e_shamen|Samana}} called this art {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}—to subdue a man's desires by enduring hunger; starve long enough, and desire faints away. His cheeks grew lean; strange dreams shone in his sunken eyes; long nails grew upon his fingers.

He stood in silence under the fierce sun until he no longer felt pain or thirst; he stood in the rain, water running over his stiff, cold shoulders and legs, until sensation was wholly extinguished; he lay prone among thorns, blood dripping, wounds festering, and still lay rigid and motionless until the sting itself ceased.

He practised also to lessen the breath and slow the heartbeat, until the heartbeat grew so faint it almost vanished. Passing through towns he saw merchants at trade, princes at the hunt, lovers meeting, and found it all not worth a glance—the world was full of suffering; life was pain, and all the world's people suffered.
The elder taught them self-mastery and meditation. {{e_laoshamen|the eldest Samana}} was nearly sixty, dust in his tangled hair, his temper like thunder in the woods.
Straighten your backs! If you cannot even govern your breath, how will you govern your heart? Pain is your teacher—endure it; do not hide! Whoever hides is not fit to be a Samana!

In meditation the soul of [[NPC1]] flew from his body. A grey eagle swept over the bamboo; he became that eagle, flying over forest and mountain, hunting fish, enduring an eagle's hunger, speaking an eagle's tongue, dying an eagle's death. A dead jackal lay on the sand; his soul slipped into that carcass, lay there swelling, stinking, rotting, torn by hyenas, pecked by vultures, becoming remnant and dust, dissolving into the air. He killed his senses, wiped out his memory, fled into a thousand forms of the world—he was animal, corpse, rock, wood, water.

Yet each time he woke again in sunlight or moonlight, became himself again, felt again the restlessness of longing—no matter how far he fled, he always came back to himself, and he had found no peace. The elders praised him as the harshest in practice, the swiftest to learn, their proudest disciple. But in this young man's heart a secret doubt of the meaning of it all was stirring.

cards.title: Anesthetic

segments.text: Three years. In the {{e_kuxiulin|forest of the Samanas}} I have learned every art of the Samanas: meditation, the governing of breath, {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}—starving for so long that desire faints. I have tried many different paths of practice, a thousand times cast off the self and sunk into dream, yet in the end I always return to the self, and feel again the parched emptiness within.

My cheeks have hollowed; my nails are long and cracked; passers-by step aside when they see me. The elders praise me as the harshest in practice, the swiftest to learn; they say I shall one day become a saint. But today I must admit something to myself.

What is meditation? What is the sharpening of oneself by renouncing the body? Strip it bare, and it is only flight from the self, a brief escape from the quest of life, a temporary anesthetic forged from the body's pain. A cowherd sits in a tavern, drinks a few bowls of rice wine, and sinks into sleep—he is performing the same flight: no longer feeling the self, no longer feeling the pain of life. The place he reaches with one bowl of wine, we reach by starving a month, sitting a month.

Of course, when the drinker wakes, everything is as it was; he has gained nothing. And I? A thousand times I have fled the self, dwelt in nothingness, dwelt in the body of a grey eagle and a dead jackal, and each time I have been led back to myself, to feel again the restlessness of longing. Three years, and I am still like a newborn infant, as far as ever from what I wish to find.

Perhaps {{e_atman|Atman}}—that undying true Self in the heart of man—does not lie on such a road of bodily flight at all. Intoxicate the self a hundred times; when you wake, it is still sitting there waiting for me. The suffering of the body cannot bring release of the spirit. Perhaps I have been using an anesthetic all along, trying to escape my sickness. I do not want to go on like this.

cards.title: The Rising Spiral

segments.text: Once, on the road out of the forest to beg food, the two young men walked one behind the other. [[NPC2]] spoke suddenly.
Tell me, are we on the right path? Are we growing in wisdom, drawing nearer to our goal? Or are we—only going in circles?

Why do you think that again? We have learned much, and we are still learning. We are not going in circles; we are going upward—our path of seeking is a rising spiral, and we have already climbed many steps. The elder often praises you; he says you will one day be a great Samana.
Our venerable elder—how old is he this year?
About sixty, I suppose. Why?

He is sixty, and he has still not attained {{e_niepan|Nirvana}}—that still realm beyond birth and death, where all unrest is extinguished. He will practise until seventy, until eighty, and still not reach it. You and I will grow old the same way, fasting and meditating the same way, and fall equally short. I do not think a single Samana among them all will attain Nirvana. We have found a little comfort, learned a few conjurer's tricks, and only deceive ourselves, that is all.
Do not say such terrible things! So many scholars, so many devout ascetics, so many who have devoted themselves—can it be that not one of them has found the right path?

Year after year I sought instruction from the wise among the Brahmins, from the sacred {{e_feituo|Vedas}}—the scriptures handed down through our generations, the wellspring of sacrifice and wisdom. Yet it has taken me this long to understand: a man cannot obtain the one true thing through learning alone. Hidden in the essence of all things there is a secret that cannot be called “knowledge.”

Your words frighten me. If it is as you say, and learning is of no use, then what meaning have our devout prayers? Where does the holiness of practice stand? What in this world is still worth treasuring and revering?
I do not know, my friend. I know only that my thirst has not lessened by a fraction, and of what I seek I have not found even one part. Before long I shall leave this Samana path.
Leave? And what of us? Did we not agree that we would practise together until the day we grasped the truth?
The path I must go and seek myself now. Forgive me.

[[NPC1]] stopped on the road, raised his hands, and let them fall again, powerless. He looked at the figure ahead—always half a step faster than he—and for the first time a panic rose in him: this man, he could scarcely keep up with him any longer.

cards.title: Rumour and Hypnosis

segments.text: When the two young men had almost completed three years with the Samanas, rumours poured into this jungle from every side: a sage of the Sakya clan had appeared. It was said he had conquered the world's sufferings and forever stilled the wheel of rebirth—men call the ceaseless turning of life between birth and death {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}, a wheel that never stops; and he had passed beyond it, reached {{e_niepan|Nirvana}}, that still farther shore where all unrest is extinguished. They called him “the Enlightened One”—a man who had awakened.

Rumour grew wings. Some praised him for wisdom beyond compare, for remembering his former lives, for having subdued demons; others mocked him as a fraud, saying he scorned sacrifice, lived in luxury, and was unlearned. The city talked; the forest talked. Every piece of news was laden with doubt and with hope, and young seekers everywhere pricked up their ears. Many believed without question, many doubted, and many set out at once to seek this sage [[NPC1]].

The elder of the jungle had no love at all for these rumours. He had heard that this “Enlightened One” had once been an ascetic too, but had given up austerity and gone back to the bustling city, to live in a fine house, and he scorned him the more.

Absurd! A man who threw off austerity halfway and went over to pleasure—and he is fit to speak of “awakening”? Whoever mentions him again shall starve three extra days! I have practised a lifetime, and I have never heard that by wallowing in the worldly, liberation would fall from the sky!

But the more the rumours were forbidden, the louder they grew. At last one day the two young men came together before the elder and asked leave to quit the jungle, to hear with their own ears the teaching of that Enlightened One.
What? Both of you leaving? Ungrateful creatures! I taught you the arts one by one, and this is how you repay me? Get out! Get out now!
[[NPC4]] started in alarm and stepped back again and again. [[NPC3]] leaned to his companion's ear and said softly—
Do not be afraid. Now I will let this old man see what I have learned from him.

With that he approached the elder, stood still, and fixed his whole attention on the old man's eyes. With his look he seized the old man, hypnotised him, conquered his will, and silently commanded him to obey. The old man fell suddenly silent, his gaze froze, his arms hung powerless; all that fire could not issue a spark—this art of capturing the soul was what the old man himself had taught, year after year.
Then the old man bowed again and again to the two young men, blessed them, and stammered a few words of safe journey. They thanked him, bowed in return, and set out empty-handed.
I can scarcely believe my eyes… You hypnotised an elder—that is the hardest, hardest thing of all! I tell you truly, if you stayed, you would soon learn to walk on water!
I have no mind to walk on water. Let those who have grown old and rotten be content with such cheap tricks.
The morning mist thinned; two figures took the road toward the great city. The man of the rumours was still far away, yet both of them felt they had already heard his voice.

cards.title: The Teaching at Jetavana

segments.text: Asking the way as they went, the two young ascetics entered {{e_sheweicheng|Savathi}}. The one walking in front was named {{e_xidaduo|Siddhartha}}. The Enlightened One—people called him “the Buddha,” meaning “the awakened one”—was a household name in this city; every house was willing to fill a monk's {{e_boyu|alms bowl}} with food. The two young men stood silently begging at the first door, and the master of the house at once gave them food.
Kind woman, please tell us: where does the Blessed One dwell? We are Samanas from the forest, come to pay our respects to this holy man, in the hope of hearing the teaching from his own mouth.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Ah, Samanas from the forest. The Blessed One lives in the monastery outside the city—a wealthy elder bought the whole grove and offered it to him; those who come to hear the teaching may spend the night there. Every day I see him in a yellow robe, walking the lanes in silence, holding out his bowl at the doors, and carrying the bowl back again.

The two thanked her and took their leave, and followed the stream of pilgrims to that great grove. Deep shade covered the sun; monks were as many as clouds, like a little town: some sat under trees in silent absorption, some gathered in fierce debate. They were all disciples of {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—the company of wandering monks who follow the Buddha, wearing the {{e_sengyi|yellow robe}}, keeping the precepts, taking one meal a day at noon.
It was already late in the day. The two young men first found a sheltered corner, meaning to rest until dawn and then see with their own eyes the man of the rumours.

At morning [[NPC1]] went quietly out of the grove gate with his bowl to beg food. He walked among hundreds of monks dressed alike, and at first glance nothing about him seemed unusual, yet Siddhartha knew him at once. There was no pride in the man; his peaceful look was neither joy nor sorrow, as if a mild smile rose from within—a smile no different from a newborn child's.
His face, his gait, his gaze, even each of his fingers, spoke of completeness, and held a stillness that nothing could destroy.

He did not speak a word; merely by walking so quietly, he made himself known. The two young Samanas followed at a distance, watched him enter the city, watched him return, watched him withdraw into the shade of a mango tree with food enough only to feed a bird. They decided to fast that day.
At dusk the heat receded; those sleeping in the open gathered under the trees. That voice rose, clear and peaceful, like the motion of light, like stars in the night sky—
Life is suffering. Suffering has its origin; the origin can be extinguished; extinction has its path. I have found this path. If you walk it, you too can put an end to all pain.
He spoke of “suffering, origin, cessation, and the path,” patiently, with parables, repeating it again and again. The two young men listened until late into the night; neither moved a step.

cards.title: The Night of Taking Refuge

segments.text: When the teaching in the grove ended, the night was already deep. Among those sleeping in the open, many pilgrims came forward and asked to join {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—the company of monks who follow the Buddha, wander the four directions, and keep the precepts. {{e_qiaodamo|Gotama}} looked at them and received them one by one.
You have listened to the teaching with great care. Then follow us, enter the garden of bliss, and put an end to all pain.
Not far off, that friend who had always been shy—[[NPC1]]—suddenly pressed forward as well. His voice was tight, but there was no hesitation.
I… I wish to take refuge in the Blessed One, in your teaching. Please receive me, and let me be one of the order.
He too was received. When he turned, he remembered to look anxiously for his friend, only to find that his friend had not stepped forward with him.

We have both heard the Blessed One teach, and have felt this peace. I have already taken it to heart and will practise it, following him—will you not stay too, and walk the path of salvation? Is this not what we have always wanted to seek? Will you still delay, still wait?

My friend, you have taken that step and chosen your own path. You have always followed me; I have often wondered whether one day you could take a step without me, on your own. Now you have taken it. May you walk this path to its end; may you find your own salvation!
Speak, my dear friend—say that you too are willing to swear refuge to the Buddha! Let us stay together!
Friend, you have already heard my blessing. I say it once more: you need follow me no longer. You have found the path you long for; may you walk it, and may you find what you seek.
In an instant [[NPC1]] understood: the one he had followed since his youth, his dearest friend, was about to leave him. His tears welled up.

Do not grieve; you now belong to the Buddha's order. You have given up home and parents, birth and wealth, you have given up friendship too, and your former choices—but this is truly your own heart's wish. Tomorrow I shall leave you.

The two friends walked a long time in the grove, lay down, and still could not sleep. Again and again he asked why his friend would not take refuge; the other only waved his hand and would not say. At dawn an old monk called the newly received together and distributed the {{e_sengyi|yellow robe}}—to put it on was to bid farewell to home, wealth, and the old self.
[[NPC1]] embraced the friend of his youth and put on the yellow robe. From then on he stayed, walking his own path, and was no longer anyone's shadow.

cards.title: The Crack in the Teaching

segments.text: The next day the young man met the Blessed One in the grove. He greeted him with respect and gathered courage to ask for speech. The Blessed One silently consented.
Rare Blessed One, yesterday I had the fortune to hear your profound teaching. My friend has taken refuge with you, and I shall continue my own seeking.
As you wish.
My words may be rash, yet I would not leave without telling you my thought. Will you hear a few sentences more?
Speak.

What I most revere in your teaching is its perfection and its clarity. You have shown this world as a complete, unbroken chain, linked by the cycle of cause and effect. Never before has the world been so clearly described: not determined by chance, nor by the gods, but link upon link, each the law of the other.

And yet in this rounded unity there is a small crack. Your teaching, so exquisite and beyond the world, cannot be shown, cannot be proved; it can only be realised by one who has lived it—and through this, a small gap appears. Forgive me for raising this objection.
The Blessed One had listened in stillness, without moving. Then he answered in a voice kind, humble, and clear.

You have listened with great care, descendant of Brahmins; that is praiseworthy. But do not fall into the abyss of disputation. Words may be beautiful or ugly, clever or foolish; anyone may accept them or refuse them. My teaching is not a set of arguments; its aim is not to explain this world to anyone, but to help all rise out of suffering and obtain salvation. That is all.

Please do not be angry; I did not wish to dispute with you over words. I have never for a moment doubted that you have attained awakening. But you reached the goal by your own seeking and experience, through thought and awakening—you did not learn it from a doctrine either. Therefore I believe no one can obtain salvation by learning a doctrine. The experience of the moment you awoke cannot be conveyed to anyone in words and doctrine.

Your teaching embraces much: how to live rightly, how to turn from evil, how to still {{e_lunhui|Samsara}} and reach {{e_niepan|Nirvana}}, that still farther shore where all unrest is extinguished. But one thing the teaching cannot contain: the secret of what you yourself experienced on the road to awakening.

That is exactly why I am resolved to keep walking my own path—I shall leave all doctrines and teachers, walk it myself, experience it myself, and reach my goal. O rare Blessed One, I shall often remember this moment: I saw with my own eyes a holy man standing before me, and I have seen that someone can find his own path.
The Blessed One's gaze lowered; his unfathomable expression showed a complete stillness.

I hope your reasoning is not mistaken. But tell me: you have seen my order and the brothers who have taken refuge—do you think they would do better to abandon the teaching and return to a world ruled by desire?

I never had such a thought! May they all follow your teaching and reach their own goals. I have no right to judge another man's life; I can judge only for myself. If I too became your disciple, I fear it would remain only on the surface—I would deceive myself that I had already been saved, while in truth I would not have satisfied the self's need to go on growing.
The Blessed One gazed at this unknown young man, with a hint of a smile, and with a gesture almost imperceptible signed him to withdraw.
You are clever, Samana from afar; you know how to argue with skill. My friend—beware of your own excessive cleverness.
The Blessed One walked slowly away. That smile was engraved from then on in the depths of the young man's memory.

cards.title: Awakening

segments.text: The moment I walked out of {{e_qiyuan|Jetavana}}, I left my former life behind me as well. I walked slowly, alone, and suddenly understood: I was no longer a youth, but had stepped into maturity. Something had been shed from me, as a snake sheds its old skin—the wish to seek teachers and listen to doctrines.

The thing I wanted to learn from teachers, which they could not teach me—it is the self. I had always wanted to be rid of the self, to conquer the self, yet I never managed to face it; I only deceived it, fled from it. Of all things, what I know least is precisely myself.

Why? For one reason only: I feared the self; I was fleeing the self. I sought {{e_atman|Atman}} with my whole heart—that undying true Self, one with the universe—wanting to destroy the self and find the core of all things in its ruins. And precisely because of that, I lost myself along the way.

At last I have seen a great man, before whom I must lower my eyes in homage. No other teaching can attract me any more, since this man's teaching, so exquisite, did not persuade me either. Though he has taken my friend—my friend who once believed in me and followed me, and now believes in him and follows him—he has given me something of greater worth: the finding of the self.
Though I now stand as lonely as a fixed star in space, I am more firmly resolved than ever before to become myself.

From today everything is reversed: I will no longer flee myself, no longer practise any doctrine. I will learn from the self, take the self as teacher, and face its feelings. I am no longer a priest, nor a Samana in flight; {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—that old road of birth and death—I have walked to its end.

I lifted my eyes and looked about, as if seeing this world for the first time: there gold, there deep blue, there green. Sky, river, forest, mountain—strangely beautiful. Meaning is not behind things; it is in the things themselves. Today I have at last awakened, and been born again. I will not go home—my road is ahead.

cards.title: The I in Rumour

segments.text: Before it is light I go out with the {{e_boyu|alms bowl}}. I have walked the lanes of this city for many years; with my eyes shut I know which flagstones are sunken. The children of the city can call my name; housewives fill the bowl with food across the threshold, and if one would add another spoonful, I ask her to take it back—one meal is enough; what is extra weighs a man down so he cannot walk.

When I hold the bowl I do not speak. Some think it is a rule. It is only this: if a man is willing to share his food with you, in that moment he already holds his own answer and his own assent in his heart, and I need say nothing more.

The stories about me grow year by year. Some say I remember every road I walked in former lives; some say I subdued spirits in the snow mountains; and some say I practised austerity in youth, then loved ease, a fraud who quit halfway. When such words come back to the grove, the young disciples flush with anger and want to go and argue with the speakers.

I say: let it be. Rumour itself grows old and changes; it is nothing to mind. What truly matters is another thing—this year the people sleeping under the trees of my grove are twice last year's number.

That is what truly worries me. Many of them have come for tales of wonder, wanting to see me take a step on water, wanting to hear me speak of my former lives. But none of that is me; I can only speak, again and again, of 【suffering】, of its origin, of the path that extinguishes it—slowly, at tedious length, in parables as plain as I can make them for them. Once is not enough; those who stay to hear it a second time have usually truly taken it in.

This morning at the city gate there were two young men out of the woods. Thin, dirty, yet their eyes bright. They did not press forward with the crowd to pay respects; they only followed me at a distance, all the way to the grove gate. I know such men: they have not come to take refuge; they have doubts of their own in their hearts, and have come to test me. The best disciples in {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}} are often of this kind; there are exceptions too—many who, having heard me, turn away and never come back in a lifetime.

That is well also. This business of seeking the way was never about me leading anyone. Each man has his own path, and each must find it himself; I have only arrived a step sooner, and turned back, wishing to point out the road under my feet to those still walking.

cards.title: Lay Out One More Robe

segments.text: As the summer heat receded, the people in the grove began to gather toward the central clearing, waiting for the discourse. An elder monk, carrying a newly washed and sunned {{e_sengyi|yellow robe}}, walked quickly to the tree.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: Blessed One, tonight I fear there will not be room to sit. The eastern clearing is full as well, and people are still standing outside the woods. Shall I ask them to come back tomorrow?
No need. Room is made by people pressing together. Go and say: those sitting near, draw in your legs a little and squeeze closer; those sitting far, do not push forward—my voice will reach them.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: And another matter. At the distribution of food today, two young Samanas from the forest ate not a bite. When asked, they said it was voluntary {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}. It looks as if they have already starved a whole day.

Then let them starve; do not worry. They are not being polite to us; it is their own decision: in the woods they had to endure it every day, and today, come to a place where there is food, they want to starve through first, so that they may sit down and listen with a quiet mind.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: I do not understand. Hearing the teaching is hearing the teaching—can one take it in on an empty stomach?
One day is nothing to a Samana. They must first make one thing clear: what I can give here is not the worldly, not a good meal.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: …Then what is it you give?
A path. I only point out the path underfoot; whether they walk it depends on their own legs, on their own thoughts.
The elder monk still wanted to ask, and swallowed the words. He looked at the dark press of heads in the clearing and suddenly sighed.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: Today again someone came asking for wonders. Said he wanted to see you take a step on water, and only then would he believe the rumours.
What did you answer?

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: I said we do not do that here. They laughed, and asked how we were any different from Samanas elsewhere.

Well answered. I saw a few in my youth who could walk on water. They are still walking on water, and have gained no truth from it; rather the trick has bewildered them, and a whole life has simply gone by that way. Men are caught turning without end in birth, age, sickness, and death; everyone calls it {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—and those with water underfoot are likewise mired in Samsara.
He stood, straightened the edge of his robe, and walked toward the clearing. After two steps he looked back.
Tonight lay out one more robe.

segments.speaker: Elder monk
segments.text: Someone will take refuge tonight? How do you know?

The shy come earliest and stand last, but their eyes hide nothing. When I entered the grove I saw one who had already been standing there a long time: he never dared come forward, yet his eyes never left this side.

cards.title: The Missing Corner

segments.text: This morning a young man from afar stood before me, took apart what I have spoken for decades and looked it through, and then told me: a corner is missing here.

He was not wrong. He was not the first to see it, but he was the first to say it to my face, with respect. I listened and did not move. I was like that in my youth: thinking that if the reasoning were straightened, a man could stand straight too.

I did not argue with him. Arguing is easy; these two lips of mine have not lost in forty years—but if I argued him down, he would believe me all the more, and be all the less willing to walk the road he must awaken to himself. I answered him with one short sentence, as a parting gift. He will need some thirty years of walking, I think, before he knows what that sentence meant.

His friend stayed; last night he put on the yellow robe, and is now one of {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}. Some will say: the one who stayed is the duller, the one who left the cleverer. I do not see it so. The one who stayed has already finished asking his questions; the one who left must still ask them through to the end, alone. Which arrives first I do not know; I know only that both are walking their own road.

Speech is only an old cart; what it can haul is limited. I watched him walk out the gate of {{e_qiyuan|Jetavana}}, his back straight, his step very light. What I thought then was: the corner missing from the teaching may be left precisely for such as him.

cards.title: The Ferryman and the River

segments.text: After leaving the Buddha's grove, [[NPC1]] travelled several days alone. He had been a Samana, and now he had laid even that path down; his heart felt, instead, light and bright. That evening he came to a great river: the water wide, forest on both banks as far as the eye could see, dusk spreading little by little over the surface. On the shore stood a {{e_dukoucaoshe|hut at the ferry}}, a small house where the ferryman rested and received guests. He asked lodging; {{e_weisudewa|Vasudeva}} agreed readily, and shared with him bread, water, and mangoes. The fire crackled; this was the first night in many years he need not sleep in the open.

segments.speaker: Ferryman
segments.text: The night is cool; sleep by the fire. Tomorrow at first light I will take you across.

segments.speaker: Ferryman
segments.text: From your dress, you come from the woods. Where are you going?
To the great city ahead. I am a Samana no longer—from here on, the road I will walk myself.

segments.speaker: Ferryman
segments.text: Good. The river never asks where she is going, yet in the end she always reaches the sea.

At first light the ferryman set his bamboo pole; the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}—more like a great bamboo raft—slid into midstream. The wide water held a peach-coloured dawn; the {{e_yezishu|palm shore}} receded quietly in the thin mist. He had never looked at a river so; for a moment he was lost in it.
This is a beautiful river.

segments.speaker: Ferryman
segments.text: It is. I love it more than anything. It has kept me company for many years; I often listen to it murmur, or gaze at it in stillness. A man can learn a great deal from a river.
They reached the bank. [[NPC1]] felt in his empty pocket, a little ashamed.
Thank you, kind man. I fear I have no ferry-money for you—I have nothing.

segments.speaker: Ferryman
segments.text: I can see that, and I did not expect your money. One day you will come and repay me. That too I learned from this river: the water flows away and flows back; it always returns. A safe journey to you; may your friendship be my reward.

The words were strange, yet oddly kind. [[NPC1]] smiled, said farewell, and took it for a joke. He did not yet know that he would remember this morning and this river many years later; still less what the ferryman's “repay” would mean. He knew only that everyone he met on the road was well-disposed and willing to be his friend; in his eyes, people were like children.

cards.title: The Lady in the Palanquin

segments.text: Before he entered the city, [[NPC1]] came upon a train of menservants and maids beside a beautiful unwalled garden outside the walls: each carried a gift-box. In the middle of the procession was a splendid palanquin borne by four men, a coloured awning, a crimson cushion, gold thread on the curtains. He had lived three years in the woods by begging; never had he seen such state. He stood at the garden entrance and watched the procession approach in its splendour.

In the palanquin sat a lady, [[NPC2]]. Beneath a high coil of hair was a face both brilliant and intelligent: a small mouth, crimson, like a newly picked fig; the brows drawn cleverly into an arc; a pair of black eyes, clever and keen; the neck smooth and long. She wore a gown of bright green and gold; wide gold bracelets on her wrists; in her hand a {{e_kongqueshan|peacock fan}} stirred lightly, the eye-spots on the feathers flashing.

He had never seen such beauty; his heart filled with joy. As the palanquin passed him he bowed low; when he rose he met those intelligent eyes. For an instant the beautiful woman inclined her head and smiled, then vanished with her servants into the depths of the garden. He stood where he was, greedily breathing the unknown perfume that lingered in the air, his heart beating hard—a feeling so strange to him.

A longing and a stirring rose through his whole body, but he had never touched a woman before, and this unfamiliar feeling bewildered him. In that instant he heard the voice of his own heart, and he was glad to be in touch with people again; he had lived in the forest too long.

segments.speaker: Servant
segments.text: Out of the way! What dirty Samana is this, blocking the garden gate, staring at the lady?

The servants' looks, scornful and dismissive, came at him like needles. [[NPC1]] lowered his head and for the first time examined himself with care: tangled hair full of dust, a torn loincloth barely covering him, bare feet. A shame he had never felt rose in him—in the woods he had been proud of poverty; but at this garden gate, before so beautiful a woman, he suddenly felt himself only a beggar. I cannot enter this garden like this, he thought, and could not help laughing aloud.

He asked passers-by about the garden and its mistress. She was, it seemed, of these {{e_dachengjiexiang|streets of the city}}, the most famous {{e_mingji|courtesan}}—that is, a woman of means and art who chooses her own lovers, famed for song, speech, and the arts of love, held in honour, not an ordinary woman of the streets. She was known also for a sure eye and a proud temper: many young men who came with rich gifts never even passed her garden gate. Besides this villa outside the walls she had a house in the city.

Then I have entered this city under a lucky star, he thought. That one smile had lit a fire in his heart. He came into the city and suddenly had a goal; for that goal he surveyed the whole town, wandering the maze of lanes, watching shops, crowds, palanquins coming and going. This prosperous city told him everywhere: here everyone has money, and everyone loves money. For the first time in his life he had a clear “want”: he wanted fine clothes, costly shoes, a bag full of coin—wanted to walk into that garden with dignity, and see those eyes again. At the thought he himself was startled: a man who had thrown everything away had things he wanted once more.

cards.title: A Poem for a Kiss

segments.text: The next day he shaved his beard, combed his hair, smoothed on pomade, and waited at the garden entrance in the afternoon. When the palanquin returned he had a servant announce: a young Brahmin requested an audience. The servant led him silently to a pavilion in the garden; [[NPC1]] was reclining on a couch, playing with the fan in her hand.
It was you yesterday, waiting for me outside the garden? But yesterday you still wore a beard, your long hair full of dust; today you seem another man.

You observe well; nothing escapes your eyes. I was a Brahmin's son; I left home to seek the way, and was a Samana for three years—now I have thrown even that path aside. The first person I met before I entered the city was you. You are the first woman before whom I have needed to lower my eyes in reverence, and I thank you for your beauty. I have come to ask you to be my friend and teacher: the arts in which you excel, I know nothing of.
When she heard this, she laughed aloud.

Never has such a thing happened—a Samana from the woods coming to seek instruction from me! The young men who come here, even descendants of Brahmins, all wear fine clothes, costly shoes, hair scented, purses full of gold, and gifts worth offering. Do you understand, Samana from the woods?

I understand very well. How could I fail to understand words from so lovely a mouth? But I have already begun to learn from you: yesterday I shaved my beard, put pomade on my hair, and did my best to make myself presentable. What I lack is already little—clothes, shoes, and money, that is all.
Yes, far from enough. He must have fine clothes, costly shoes, a purse full of gold, and many gifts prepared for me.

Then I will pay with what I have learned. I know how to think, I know how to wait, I know how to {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}. These trifles are not hard; I wish to be your friend and ask you to teach me the joys of love, and you will find I am a quick pupil.
Fasting—the art of starving, of subduing desire; one who can fast is not driven by hunger, and can wait in quiet. These were three arts she did not understand.
Nothing else?
Ah, yes—I can make poems as well. May I exchange a poem for a kiss?
If your poem pleases me, of course. What sort of poem?

He thought a moment, then recited in a clear voice: Toward her garden goes the beautiful mistress; at the garden's entrance stands a dark-skinned Samana; as he gazes upon that lotus blossom, deeply he bows himself low—better to offer sacrifice to her, the beautiful one, than to the gods! She clapped loudly; the gold bracelets on her wrists rang.
Your poem is quite good, dark Samana. To give you a kiss for this poem, I lose nothing at all.

With her eyes she drew him near. His lips met those red lips, just like a newly picked fig—she kissed him deeply in return; in that kiss lay so rich a learning: conquest, refusal, and temptation besides. He stood motionless, like a child, astonished that this learning should be so vast and so deep.
Then a servant entered the pavilion and whispered a few words at her ear—a guest had arrived.
Leave here quickly, and let no one see you. I will see you again tomorrow.

She had a servant bring a {{e_baichangpao|white robe}} for him, led him out of the garden by a winding path, and told him to go at once, leaving no trace. He walked out of the garden with the folded robe under his arm, well satisfied—two days in the city, and he had already kissed the most beautiful woman in it.

cards.title: The Merchant's Interview

segments.text: Introduced by the mistress of the {{e_mingjihuayuan|courtesan's garden}}, [[NPC2]] called on the richest merchant in the city. Servants led him over luxurious carpets into a hall. The master of the great house, [[NPC1]], came in quickly: greying hair, shrewd and guarded eyes, sensual lips—a man who took business as his life. Before he spoke he looked the visitor over from head to foot. Host and guest greeted each other as friends.
I hear you are a Samana, a learned man. Yet you come seeking to serve a merchant—then you are in difficulties, I suppose?
No. I have never been in difficulties. I have no property; if that is what you mean, I have nothing, of course—but I am so by choice, therefore I am not in want.
But you have nothing; how do you live? Always on other men's property?
For nearly three years I have had not a coin, and never thought of the question. Besides, a merchant also lives by other men's property, does he not?
True. But a merchant does not take others' goods for nothing; he exchanges his own. You have nothing; what do you give? What have you learned that you can give?
Everyone gives what he has: the soldier gives strength, the teacher instruction, the farmer rice, the fisherman fish. As for me—I know thought, I know waiting, I know {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}.
Is that all? Then of what use is fasting?

Of great value. When a man has nothing to eat, the wisest thing is to fast. If I could not fast, I should have to scramble today to find some work, because hunger would drive me to act. As it is, I can wait in quiet, without haste, without want, keeping hunger at a distance for a long time, mocking hunger. So fasting is of use, sir.
A sharp tongue. But in my house, skill of the mouth will not buy a meal.
Then please try the skill of my hands.

The merchant brought a document and ordered him to read it aloud on the spot. It was a contract of sale; he looked at the page and read it through, not a word wrong. The merchant then handed him paper and brush and asked him to write a few sentences. He took up the brush, wrote, and gave it back.
The merchant unfolded the paper and saw two lines: Writing, though fair, is not so fair as thought; wit, though fair, is not so fair as patience.
Written indeed with brilliance! … We have much still to discuss. Today I invite you first as a guest, to stay in my house.

In this interview, the one being tested was unhurried, while the examiner was the first to take an interest. From then on servants brought him clothes and shoes, and attended him at the bath each day; in the rich merchant's house there were two fine, plentiful meals a day, yet he took only one, and touched neither meat nor wine. He listened much and spoke little, remembering the garden mistress's counsel—not to be a servant full of servility, but an equal counterpart. The merchant had judged countless men, and for the first time met a hireling who did not take his rice-bowl as a serious matter; astonished and admiring, and moved by his cleverness too, he gradually put important letters and papers into his hands. The servants said privately: this new guest was more like another master of the house.

cards.title: Love and Commerce

segments.text: In those years [[NPC1]] lived a full life in the city. At the appointed hour each day he put on fine clothes and costly shoes and went to visit [[NPC3]]—a woman beautiful and clever, whose profession was love. With her he passed from a child who knew nothing of love to her proudest pupil, lover, and friend.

One who cannot give pleasure will not receive it. Every gesture, every caress, every look has its own secret. After delight, one must go on admiring one another, then part with grace—so there is no satiety, and none of that terrible sense of using or being used.
He learned quickly; every lesson pleased her. Yet only she herself vaguely felt: this man took everything as a lesson; his heart was hidden away in his own depths, and never truly opened to anyone.

And in business he was more of an outsider still. His master [[NPC2]] was cautious and small in his cares, glad of a deal, anxious over a shipment, wrinkles gathering on his brow, sleepless at night, taking profit and loss as his life; he treated it only as a game—the rules he did his best to learn, the game itself never moved his heart. When he won, he smiled mildly; when he lost, he only smiled as well: a wretched transaction.

Once the master sent him to a village to buy a lot of rice. When he arrived, the rice had already been bought by another merchant. He was not angry; he simply stayed in the village: he entertained the farmers, gave the children small coins, and went to a lively wedding; a few days later he returned, well satisfied.
You have come back empty-handed! The rice is gone, and you stayed several days for nothing—wasting my time and my money!

Do not scold, my dear friend; scolding solves nothing. Since a loss has been suffered, let me bear it. I am very satisfied with this journey: I met many people, children sat on my knee and played, farmers showed me their fields—no one took me for a merchant.
All that is well enough. But you are in fact a merchant! Did you make this journey only for amusement?

Of course I went for amusement; why not? On this trip I made new friends, and gained friendship and trust. If it had been you, seeing the business could not be done, you would have hurried back in a temper, and time and money would truly have been lost. If one day you feel I have harmed your affairs, you need only say so, and I will go my own way. Until that day comes, let us remain good friends!
The master looked at him, angry and helpless—this hireling never feared a loss, yet success always fell into his hands of its own accord; a strange thing.

The labours, troubles, and pleasures of ordinary people seemed to him as mysterious and bright as the moon in the sky. He accepted all that people brought him. The merchant who came to sell him linen he welcomed, and so too the man who came to ask for a loan. He was even willing to spend a whole hour with a beggar, listening to tales of wretched hardship. All these games, and the passion that went into playing them with people, occupied all his thoughts.

Love and commerce turned like a wheel, round after round. Some call this cycle {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}: life turning without cease between birth and death, a man trapped in the wheel, still thinking he is going forward. Even the {{e_touzi|dice}} at the gambling table he played without a change of face, staking a fortune on a throw—money to him was only a counter in a game. No one knew how many more turns this game would take, or in which year it would end.

cards.title: Death of the Songbird

segments.text: One night, after years of sinking, [[NPC1]] and [[NPC2]] sat under a tree in the garden. Her look was grave; sadness and weariness could not be hidden in her speech. She asked him to tell again the story of {{e_qiaodamo|Gotama}}—that Enlightened One people call the Buddha; Buddha meaning “the awakened one.” How clear his eyes, how peaceful his smile, how complete his bearing—she could never hear enough.

One day, perhaps before long, I too shall become a disciple of this Buddha. I will offer my garden to his order—those monks in yellow robes who wander with their bowls. I want to find consolation for the heart in his teaching.

Yet having said this, she drew him to love. That time her eyes held tears; with extreme passion she clasped him violently in her arms, as if to wring the last drop of sweetness from this impermanent joy. For the first time he read the fine wrinkles at the corners of her eyes, like autumn and evening; in his own black hair there were already threads of white. He left her with a sigh, his heart full of pain and a fear he could not name.

It was the dread of old age, the dread of death. He was no longer young. Suddenly, and with perfect clarity, he saw that he was living an absurd life, that much of what he did was only play. True, he was very merry; yet real life had passed him by. He merely watched the world and amused himself with it, and his heart was not in it at all.

That night, in his own house, he kept company with dancing girls and wine, and did not go to bed until after midnight. He was long since not the man he had been: he had become a gambler to be feared, staking a fortune on one throw of the {{e_touzi|dice}}, squandering money to vent his contempt for it. He had grown weary and restless, and his heart was full of a pain he could not name.

Toward dawn he at last drifted into sleep and dreamed: the {{e_jinlongniao|songbird in the golden cage}} she kept in a small gold cage, which used to sing sweetly every morning, was silent this morning. He thought it strange, and looked close into the cage: the little bird lay stiff at the bottom, already dead. He held the dead bird in his hand a while, then threw it into the road—and in that same instant he was struck with terror, his heart wrung as by a hand, as if he had thrown away with this dead bird everything in himself that was good and of worth.

Waking from the dream he was swallowed by a great sorrow, sick to the point of vomiting, as if he had drunk sour, spoiled wine. He loathed the scented hair, the wine on his breath, the slack skin—and loathed himself more. He felt he had wasted his life without worth, without meaning, like a survivor of shipwreck on the shore.
Gloomy, he went into his own garden, shut the gate tight, and sat a whole day beneath a mango tree. As he sat there he felt himself dying, withering.

He began to review his life from the beginning: the praise of his boyhood, the austerities in the woods, the morning he heard the teaching… Had he left all those people only to become an ordinary rich man like this? When night fell he rose, bade farewell to the mango tree, to the garden, to this city, and did not return.

When she heard he had vanished, she was not surprised—she had long foreseen this day. She went silently to the gold cage by the window, opened the little door, and lifted out the bird. The bird flew lightly away; she watched a long time as it vanished in the far sky.

cards.title: Om at the Riverbank

segments.text: After leaving the city, [[NPC1]] wandered into the forest, not knowing the way. He knew only one thing: he could not go back. That life he had tasted to the point of nausea—the songbird in the cage was dead, and the songbird in his heart was dead as well. He had sunk deep into {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}: life turning like a wheel, desire following pain, pain following desire; and now this wheel held for him only nausea and a dead air.

He longed eagerly for emptiness, for peace, for death. Let a bolt of lightning destroy him! Let a tiger devour him! In this immense self-loathing, nothing in the world could any longer attract him, give him pleasure, or comfort him.

He came to a great river in the woods. Many years before, a ferryman had taken him across this same river to this same bank—he had been in his prime then, just leaving the Buddha's city. Now he was old, and stood hesitating on the bank, made very weak by weariness and hunger. Why go on? Where to? For what? Every aim had worn away; only one deep longing remained: to end this bitter life that so sickened his heart.

On the bank stood a great coconut palm. He put his arms around the trunk and leaned over, looking down at the moving water. The cold and loneliness in the water mirrored the terrible emptiness in his soul. One thought filled his heart: let go, and sink. He had come to the end of the road; only one thing was left to do—to wipe himself out, to destroy the husk of this failed life.
Let the fish in the water eat me! Eat this scoundrel, this madman—this decaying, corrupted flesh, this idle, dissipated soul!

With a twisted look he stared at the water and saw his own slack face in it. He spat at the reflection; his arms loosened from the trunk, his body slid forward; he shut his eyes and threw himself toward—death.

In that instant, from some distant corner of his soul, from the far past of his weary life, a sound came. The sound was only one word, one syllable. He recited it, indistinctly, without thinking: {{e_om|Om}}—the ancient opening and closing word of Brahmin prayer, the most sacred syllable, meaning “completeness,” which Brahmin children learn to say from the first.

In that instant the long-sleeping soul woke with a start. At once he saw how foolish his act had been: that he should be so lost, so astray, as to seek death! That he should think to buy peace by destroying the body! The shock of that word entering his heart exceeded all the torment, disillusion, and despair of these years put together. He saw clearly his wretched state, and perceived also that life cannot be destroyed.

But it lasted only a moment. Weariness overwhelmed him; he sank down under the great tree, his head on the roots, reciting that word in a low voice as he fell into a deep sleep. The sleep was deep and without dreams; he had not slept so in a very long time.
He had meant to drown himself in this river. In truth, that aged, weary, despairing self had already drowned in it.

cards.title: How Beautiful the World Is

segments.text: How beautiful the world has suddenly become! At morning I watch the sun rise beyond forest and mountain; at evening I watch the far sunset; at night I look up at the stars, and see the sickle moon like a little boat drifting on the dark sky. Gold, deep blue, green—this many-coloured world has been here all along: sun, moon, and stars forever shining, rivers forever running, bees forever humming.
Once I took it all for empty, impermanent illusion, destined to be despised and discarded by thought. But now my eyes are enamoured of this world, and I will seek my own place in it.

When a man looks with a child's simple, wishless gaze, intent upon the present, life is truly a delight. Thought and the senses are of equal weight—behind both something ultimate is hidden. I will listen to both voices with equal care, despising neither, overvaluing neither. All the things of this human world I will truly feel; I must win my own experience.

I knew long ago that my self is {{e_atman|Atman}}—the undying true Self in the depths of a man—yet I never truly found it, because I always wanted to catch it in the net of thought. From now on I will obey only the voice in my own heart, without delay, without hesitation. I will no longer turn to austerity, sacrifice, bathing, and prayer; I refuse the drive of any outer force; I will feel my own need and wait for the moment of awakening to arrive.

It is dark. I hear the {{e_linzhongdukou|ferry in the woods}} is ahead; on the bank stands a {{e_dukoucaoshe|hut at the ferry}}, the ferryman's little house for guests, with bread and water inside. Tonight I will lodge there—for the first time in many years I am no longer afraid of an empty tomorrow.
