cards.title: I Am No Longer a Beggar

segments.text: The first thing upon entering the city: to shed my Samana skin. At the {{e_hebianshiji|stone steps by the river}}—the stone stairs of the watercourse at the city's edge—I made the acquaintance of a barber's helper: first I watched him busy in the shadow of an arch, then met him praying in a temple; I told him stories of the gods, and he listened, rapt. At first light I asked him to help me shave my beard, comb my hair, and smooth on the finest pomade, and then I bathed in the river. When the water poured over my head I felt that Samana with his dusty long hair flowing away, little by little, with the current.

Standing before a tavern where travellers gathered, I silently held out my bowl and begged a rice cake. The cake in my hand, I was suddenly startled by myself: I was a Samana no longer; why was I still begging? A pride I had never felt seized me. I actually threw the cake to a dog, and stood straight, belly empty. Perhaps tomorrow I will no longer need to beg—a man who will not beg again must first learn not to put out his hand like a beggar; I must earn money myself. From today I am no longer a beggar.

The people here live so simply, without a single difficulty. When I was a Samana, everything in my head was hardship and unrest, and at last despair; now everything is easy, easy as a newborn's first babbling. I need clothes, shoes, and money, that is all—small aims, too small to disturb a man's sleep.

These {{e_dachengjiexiang|streets of the city}}, shops, feasts, gambling, men and women in an endless stream, a playground of the world—I have come. This time I have not come to look on; I will live it.

cards.title: The Courtesan's Introduction

segments.text: The next day he called on her again. Hearing he had not eaten in two days, she took him strolling through the bustling town, dined with him, and then spoke of the business at hand.
Things are going well. {{e_shiwami|Kamaswami}} is expecting your visit—he is the richest merchant in the city; I have already mentioned you to him through others. Be clever, dark Samana!
Thank you. Then how should I treat him?

Be friendly; he has much power. But do not be too humble—I do not want you as his servant; I want you as his equal counterpart, or I shall be displeased. He is already growing old and lazy; if you please him, he will trust you greatly.
I have noted it: be a counterpart, not a servant.
Eat something first. I hear you have not eaten in two days—thinking, waiting, and fasting will not fill a belly.
They will. One who can fast is not driven by hunger. But I will not refuse your food.
You are fortunate. See, door after door is opening for you. How does it happen? Have you some magic?

Yesterday I told you I can think, wait, and fast; you thought these of no use. You will understand: when a man has an aim, he is like a stone thrown into water; he finds the swiftest line to the bottom. I do nothing; I only wait, think, fast, and let myself sink—the day before yesterday I was a slovenly beggar, yesterday I kissed the most beautiful woman, and soon I shall be a merchant and have money. That is what people call magic.
Perhaps it is as you say, my friend. But if there were no me? Without my help, where would you be now?

When I first saw you at your garden gate I had already taken the first step. I resolved to learn from the most beautiful of women the secrets of love—the moment I decided, I knew it would be fulfilled. From the first look you cast at me, I knew you would help me.
And if I had not wished to help you?
But you did wish to.

She listened in stillness. He was indeed young and handsome; she liked his voice, liked his gaze—as the cleverest {{e_mingji|courtesan}} in the whole city, she was used to men who came with purses to seek pleasure; this was the first who spoke with her of “aims” and “magic.” At parting he kissed her, and said he hoped his gaze would always give her joy, and that good fortune would come because of her.

cards.title: Writing, Though Fair

segments.text: A strange interview. That grey-haired merchant examined me through and through: asked whether I was in want, asked how I lived, then had me read a contract and write. I took up the brush and wrote him a sentence: “Writing, though fair, is not so fair as thought; wit, though fair, is not so fair as patience.” He read it twice, his eyes bright, and at once kept me as a guest at {{e_fushangzhaidi|Kamaswami's house}}—that great house, carpets laid to the door, servants in flocks, money flowing in and out of the counting-room day and night. An interview that bought food, clothing, and a place to stay—not by pleading, but by a few lines.

In truth I gave nothing, only a few things that cannot be seen. They do business by impulse and passion: glad over a shipment, anxious over an account, wrinkles gathering on the brow, sleepless at night. But I treat business as a game—the rules I learn with care, winning and losing I do not take to heart. Before long the important letters and papers were in my hands; even in urgent matters he grew used to consulting me first. He never saw through me, and often said to his friends: this Brahmin never fears a loss, yet success always falls to him—has he some magic about him?

Thought, waiting, {{e_zhaijie|fasting}}—these three arts are worth more than a boat of goods. One who can fast is not driven by hunger, and can sit steady at the table until the other party grows anxious first; a hungry man makes no good bargain, a hasty man strikes no good price. This the “foolish” Samanas in the woods taught me. The city people do not understand; they call it magic. In truth there is no magic in the world—to think, to wait, to fast, anyone can practise.

cards.title: You Do Not Know True Love

segments.text: Another dusk. These years he often came to see her at the appointed hour; the lessons of love had long been finished, yet they still liked to talk so, at length. After delight she leaned down and gazed a long time at his face, at those eyes that had grown weary. In the gold cage by the pavilion the {{e_jinlongniao|songbird in the golden cage}} too had fallen quiet.
You are the finest of all my lovers. You are stronger than the others, quicker, and more tractable—you have mastered my arts well.
You teach well, my teacher.
Do you know how many have come to me with purses full of gold, and I have never taught them so? One day, when I am a little older, I would like to have a child with you.
He was silent. She looked at him, then suddenly shook her head a little.
And yet, my dear, you are still a Samana. You do not truly love me—you love no one, is that not so?
Perhaps. I am much like you—you too have no capacity for love, or how could you practise love as an art? Perhaps people like us have none.
And ordinary people? They all seem to love with great heat.

Ordinary people can love—that is their secret. They are like fallen leaves, tumbling and drifting in the wind; we are like stars, moving on a set orbit, and the wind does not reach us. And precisely because of that, we cannot reach the joy that only fallen leaves have.
Master Star, have you ever envied the fallen leaves?
I have. They fret over children, over honour, over a little gain; that anxious, sweet intensity I cannot learn.
I cannot learn it either. I can only divide love into thirty or forty arts, and teach them one by one to men.

She was silent a long time. As the cleverest {{e_mingji|courtesan}} in the city, she was used to tender speeches; this was the first time anyone had spoken her inner case so plainly. Strangely, she was not angry.

There you are, talking like a Samana again… But you are right. In the depths of my heart there is always a still sanctuary I can withdraw into at any time, and be myself. Very few have such a sanctuary—so, like you, I cannot learn that kind of love.
At least in this moment you are my teacher, my lover, and my friend. The meaning of my present life is all here with you, not in the marketplace.

cards.title: The Potter's Wheel

segments.text: A potter's wheel, once started, will turn a long time, then slowly, and at last stop. The wheel of discernment in my soul, the wheel of thought, are the same: still turning, yet slower and slower, almost still. Worldliness and sloth seep like damp into a dying trunk, soaking my soul heavy, weary, asleep. People call this cycle {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—the days turn round after round, and a man still thinks he is living a life, when in fact he is only slowly dying.

I have learned to manage business, to give orders to servants; learned fine clothes, good wine, scented baths; learned also to gamble—the {{e_touzi|dice}} thrown, thousands won, thousands lost. Only when a great stake hung undecided did I feel a little of that terrible, sweet anxiety, feel that I was still alive. I spent to vent my contempt for money, and hated myself when day came.

Ordinary people are like children. They suffer for money, for paltry pleasures and honours, and grow grey early; they grieve bitterly over a loss a Samana would only laugh at. I envy them and despise them both—envy the strength with which they can love, despise the things they love. And I smile less and less; my face has taken on the rich man's look: sombre, irritable, never satisfied. Sometimes at night I even dream of money.

In the mirror on the bedroom wall that man grows older and uglier day by day. The world has seized him: pleasure, greed, idleness. Sometimes I think of {{e_qiaowenda|Govinda}}—that friend who always used to follow behind me. He wanders now with his bowl; has he ever failed to know himself in a mirror? And that word {{e_om|Om}}, recited from childhood, whose voice once sang aloud in my heart, now only whispers far away, almost inaudible.

cards.title: Unrecognised

segments.text: Waking, he found a shaven old monk in a {{e_sengyi|yellow robe}} sitting before him, as if sunk in meditation. The monk had neither hair nor beard; his face was aged, yet between the brows there was an eager loyalty.

You are awake? It is not good to sleep in such a place; venomous snakes and wild beasts often come here. I am a monk of {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—one of those who follow the Buddha and wander with their bowls. I was travelling with companions and saw you sleeping so deeply, so I stayed to watch over you. Later I myself fell asleep; I watched very poorly, in truth.
Thank you for watching, Samana. The Blessed One's disciples are truly very kind.
Then I will go; may you be well!
The old monk bowed farewell and turned to leave. Looking at that yellow robe, he suddenly smiled and called the other's name.
Wait—how do you know my name?!

I know you: from the Brahmin school, from the rites of sacrifice, from the years we spent together in the Samana woods, until the moment you took refuge with the Blessed One at Jetavana—I have always known you.
It is you! It is you! Why did I not recognise you just now? How glad I am to see you again!
I am very glad to see you as well. You watched over me while I slept; I thank you again—though I did not need watching.
But where are you going, old friend?
Nowhere in particular. I am still on the road; I am making a journey in search of the way.

A journey in search of the way? Forgive me—you do not look like a seeker: you wear a rich man's clothes, a gentleman's shoes; your hair is even scented. I have wandered many years, and never seen a seeker like you.

You see very truly; nothing escapes your keen eyes. But the world of appearances turns without rest; clothes and the dressing of hair change all the more. I am indeed richly dressed, because I was once rich; now I am not. As for what manner of man I am now—I do not know. In that, I am as ignorant as you.

The old monk gazed long and doubtfully at the friend of his youth, bowed as to a man of rank, and then took to the road. He watched the yellow robe go far, smiling—he still loved this loyal, ardent friend. After this sleep, how could he not love everything in the world?

Now all these impermanent things slipped away from him once more, and again he stood in the world like an infant, under the sky and on the earth, knowing nothing, owning nothing, having learned nothing. What a road it was! Merely to become a child again and begin anew, he had to go through so much folly and sin, so much error and nausea, so much disillusion and sorrow.

cards.title: One Third

segments.text: Night had fallen; the lamp in the counting-room was still lit. The master of the house, [[NPC1]], invited an old friend in the spice trade into an inner room and dismissed the servants. What he had to say concerned the lodger [[NPC2]] who had entered the house half a year before.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: You did not call me here to look at your new carpets. Speak: what is the worry?

I worry about one man. Half a year ago that {{e_mingji|courtesan}} outside the city sent word: a Samana who could write and reckon wanted a post. I thought, of what use is a Samana? Then the man came in, in a brand-new {{e_baichangpao|white robe}}, standing straight, and looked me over from head to foot first, his gaze calm yet resolute.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: A man who has begged, putting on airs. You kept him?

I did. I had him read a contract; his voice was melodious. I had him write; he wrote me a poem, and I still keep it on my desk to this day. Business he learned at once: letters, accounts, dealing with people—so clever a man, better in every way than the old hands under me.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: Then what are you worrying about?

That he does not care—I still do not know what he cares about at all. When he profits, he smiles; when he loses, he smiles as well, says the bargain was wretched, and sleeps just the same. I can go three nights without closing my eyes over a shipment; he sits beside me forever as if watching a play.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: Easy. Give him a third of the profit on what he handles, and let him bear a third of the loss as well. Once money touches a man, he wakes.
…There is reason in that. We will do it so.
A month later the two sat in the same room again. This time the master's face was longer still.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: Well? Once he had a share of the profit, he took it to heart, I suppose.

I am still the one who takes it to heart. The first deal he made a profit; he turned and gave half to the porters on the quay. The second he lost; he made it up himself without a word, then went off to someone's wedding feast. I said a couple of things to him; guess what he answered.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: What did he answer?

He said: from you I have learned what a basket of fish should sell for, what interest a loan should bring; those are your arts. But I have not learned from you how to think—that, you had better learn from me.

segments.speaker: Spice merchant
segments.text: …He dared say that? You did not send him away?

I cannot drive him away. Strange: while he is here, business runs smoothly; if he goes, I fear it will not. Tell me if it is not maddening: I get up at midnight to count the books for this trade, and he sleeps like a child every night. There are such men in this world—everything in their hands, and nothing taken as real. What on earth does such a man care about?

cards.title: At Last He Has Learned to Worry

segments.text: At first I was glad. At last he was willing to worry over money—that was what I had hoped for all these years. He began to chase debtors for payment, harder than I; once he could sit a whole hour with a beggar and even give him money, now he dismissed them from behind the door. I thought: good, now he looks like a man of business.

Later I could not laugh. It was not that he loved money; he hated it. Thousands staked on one throw of the {{e_touzi|dice}}, no joy in winning, no change in losing, and the next day he doubled the stake just the same. Fewer and fewer dared gamble against him; at last only a few strangers from elsewhere. The stakes grew larger and larger. He lost a country villa once; I redeemed it for him—the price I never dared tell him.

Now the {{e_dachengjiexiang|streets of the city}} are talking: that gentleman wins and loses ten thousand in a night without a change of face. They take it for skill. I know it is not. A man who treats money as an enemy—money will collect its due sooner or later.

All my life I have been careful, sleepless over a shipment, and he has laughed at me for ten years. But I have done nothing wrong: I take goods by the scale, pay by the contract, keep a whole household, and have never cheated anyone of a coin. He laughs at the wrinkles on my brow—the wrinkles I earned myself; no one bestowed them.

Last month I went to his room and found him staring at the mirror on the wall. That face I knew, and did not quite know: hair scented, skin slackened, the little light gone from the eyes. He saw me, smiled, and said: old friend, how is business today. I could hardly recall how he had looked when he was young.

cards.cgPrompt: a dim opulent bedchamber in ancient India at late night, seen over a gray-haired merchant's shoulder: scattered dice and coins on a carpet, a bronze mirror on the wall reflecting only lamp flame, the merchant standing small in the doorway unable to speak, wealth turned cold, melancholy amber tones

cards.title: He Left No Word

segments.text: On the third morning, the steward came in with a string of keys and a ledger. The master of the house, [[NPC1]], was at his meal. He looked up—and could eat no more. The man he wanted, [[NPC2]], had not been seen for three days.

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: Sir, there is still no sign of him. I have asked at the city gates, at the harbour, in every street and lane.
And the garden?

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: The garden gate is bolted from within; the gardener says no one has gone in for many days. A barber at the {{e_hebianshiji|stone steps by the river}} says he saw, some days ago, a gentleman in fine clothes sitting there alone, watching the water, sitting a long while. Whether it was him, he cannot say.
Out of the city? Alone? How much money did he take?

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: That is the strange part. Not a coin was touched. Here is the ledger—I have checked it three times. Not a discrepancy, not even last month's odd sums. His clothes, his rings, his shoes—all laid out in the room, neat as ever.
Settled? He settled the accounts before he left?

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: Yes. The last entry is the silk of the fourteenth. Even the wastage is counted in.

…Then he was robbed. He must have been robbed. That road beyond the city has not been safe for years—go, take more men, search toward the woods! If you find nothing, search downstream; look in the river-bends as well!

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: Sir, permit me a word. If he was robbed, why did the robbers not come into the house for the money?
The master did not answer. He opened the ledger and shut it, opened it and shut it, three times over, and at last stopped at the last line, where the pen had rested.
These last days… did he say anything to you?

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: Nothing. Only once, standing under the eaves watching the rain, he said a strange thing.
What did he say?

segments.speaker: Steward
segments.text: He said: Water that flows from here will reach the sea, sooner or later. I did not understand; I thought he meant the drain in the courtyard.
…Search. Keep searching.

They searched another half a year. The master never could understand—a man who lays down money, clothes, house and trade, and for what? He left that room empty a whole year, and had the bedding aired once a month. Only in the spring of the second year did he rent it to a stranger who sold flax.

cards.title: My Name Is Vasudeva

segments.text: At dusk the great river was in flood. A man in rich clothes came on foot, alone, to the ferry. His hair was already turning grey, and dust covered his fine robes. The old ferryman wondered to himself: men dressed like this always went out in carriages or palanquins.
Old man, will you ferry me to the other shore?
The ferryman asked him aboard the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}. The long oar dipped, and they left the bank. The guest gazed at the water, then suddenly spoke.
You have chosen a beautiful life. To live by the river every day, to travel on it every day—it must be very beautiful.
It is as you say, sir—very beautiful. And yet, sir, which life, which labour, is not beautiful?
Perhaps. Still, I envy yours.
Ah, you would soon tire of it. This is not a life for men in rich clothes.
The guest smiled. He said that today, because of these clothes, he had been questioned all along the road; he would give the fine robes to the ferryman as fare—he had not a copper on him.
You must be joking, sir.
It is no joke. Many years ago you ferried a young Samana across for nothing—Samanas, those seekers who leave their homes and wander in austerity. Today, ferry him once more.
The oar in the ferryman's hands slowed. He looked at the stranger a long while, carefully. Then a smile rose from the depths of his wrinkles.
I know you. More than twenty years ago you spent a night in my {{e_dukoucaoshe|hut at the ferry}}. You were a Samana then, and we parted as friends. I am sorry I did not keep your name.
I was a Samana then, yes.
You are welcome. My name is [[NPC1]]. Be my guest today, and sleep again in that hut—and tell me again why you have grown so weary of these fine clothes.
I am weary of them, and of everything they bought me. I want to stay here: give me an old garment; let me be a helper first, then an apprentice. I must learn to row.

They reached midstream, where the current ran hard. The ferryman asked no more; he only worked his strong arms, rising and falling, and rowed steadily. Watching him, the guest felt a solid joy he had not known in a long time.

Ashore, the guest helped him moor the boat. In the hut there was bread, clear water, and mangoes. The sun sank; the two old men sat on a log by the river. The guest told his life: birth, study, wealth, the long fall, down to today's despair, and the waking after despair beside the river. The story lasted deep into the night.

The ferryman only listened—did not interrupt, did not press, did not blame, did not praise. When he heard of the tree on the bank and the syllable that saved a life, he listened so intently that he even shut his eyes. The teller felt that every word he spoke was being patiently received, by him and by the river.

Stay, my friend. The river has known you a long time; it is kind to you. My wife has been dead many years; I have lived alone too long. Come and share this life with me—you will not want for food or shelter.
I thank you; I accept. And I thank you for this as well: in all my wanderings I have never met a man so willing to listen.
That night [[NPC2]] slept deeply in the hut. The river ran past the window, like a song that would not end. The old life was dead; the new one began here.

cards.title: The Ferryman's Apprentice

segments.text: Life settled at the ferry. Each day before dawn, the old ferryman {{e_weisudewa|Vasudeva}} woke the new apprentice. The craft was learned piece by piece: tending the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}, stopping the seams in the hull, oiling the sides of the boat, carrying passengers across; when the ferry was idle, planting rice in the fields, or gathering wood and picking bananas in the forest.
Shape the oar along the grain. Steady hands—and a steadier heart.

The apprentice did as he was told. He learned to make {{e_chuanjiang|oar}}—choosing the straightest wood, planing it, polishing it, fitting the handle to the palm; he learned to weave baskets, pressing the bamboo strips dense and even. Hands that had held only pens and wine-cups soon grew calluses.

The master's words were always short: one sentence, never a second time. Little by little the apprentice learned to read the water: clouds meant the rains were coming; eddies meant depth; driftwood told what had happened upstream. The master said none of this needed teaching; the river would speak, if one would listen.

Years ran past like the river. Slowly travellers noticed a strange thing: the smiles of the two ferrymen, old and younger, grew more and more alike—the same unfolding from a thousand fine lines, the same innocence, the same peace. Many, boarding, asked: Are you brothers? The two only looked at each other and smiled.
At dusk after work, the two old men sat on the log by the bank. The apprentice had been carrying a question for many days.
Master, have you also learned this secret from the river—that time does not exist at all?
Oh? Tell me.
The river is everywhere at once. At the source, at the waterfall, at the ferry, in the sea—each place is it, and each is only 'now'. It is not a shadow of the past, nor a shadow of the future.

My life is a river too. The boy I was, the man in his prime, the white-haired man—only three stretches drawn by illusion, not three true persons. What was is not left behind in 'the past'; death does not wait in 'the future'. The mind of the past cannot be grasped, nor the mind of the future; all is now, all is only this moment.
You have understood.

And there is another layer. I used to think men suffered in {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—birth and death turning, circle after circle, with no way out. Now I see it clearly: all sorrow, all fear, in truth live in time. Fear is fear of “later”; regret is regret for “before.” If time is seen through and one looks only at the present, what suffering is left in the world to bear?
What you used to fear was tomorrow. And now?
Now I only fear failing this moment.
Good.
Master, why did you never tell me these things of your own accord?
What others tell is only idle talk; what one tastes for oneself is experience. So I do not speak. I can sit and listen with you.
He grew more and more excited as he spoke. The master only smiled, nodded, touched his shoulder, and rose to weave a basket. That touch was warmer than a hundred praises.

When night fell, master and apprentice still sat by the river, listening. It was not the sound of water—they felt it was life itself speaking. As [[NPC1]] listened, he felt the wounds of his first half of life being soothed, little by little, by that sound.

cards.title: The Snakebite

segments.text: The news ran like wildfire: the Awakened One was gravely ill, and would soon leave the world. {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—those in yellow robes who begged with bowls and wandered in practice—hurried from all sides to his sickbed; merchants, women, and old people crowded the roads, as if to a king's coronation, or like bees drawn to a magnet. Everyone wished to see him once more. The {{e_duchuan|ferry}} at the ferry did not rest from dawn to dusk. Some said an age was ending.

In the crowd walked a mother and child. She wore plain clothes—she had once heard the Awakened One {{e_qiaodamo|Gotama}} teach in the great city, and had given him her garden; now, hearing he was dying, she had come on foot with the child to see him on his last journey. In her face one could still see that she had been the most beautiful woman in the city; the boy was about eight, in silk, with a handsome face, crying and fussing all the way—wanting rest, wanting food, bursting into anger and rudeness at every turn, or else into tears.
I can't walk any more! I want to go home! What has a dying old man to do with me?
Be good, a little longer. Once we cross this river, we shall be nearly there. Mother begs you.
It's your fault! We had a good home, and you had to come this far!

The child had been used, from infancy, to testing his mother and making mischief. She had to stop and start: feed him, soothe him, then scold him. In the woods she was so weary she curled on the ground and half-closed her eyes to rest; the child sat beside her, eating a banana with relish.
Suddenly she cried out in pain, her face gone white—a small snake was crawling out from under her.
Mother! Mother, what is it?
Don't be afraid… help Mother up. The ferry is just ahead; we will go for help.

Mother and child stumbled forward. Thorns tore her skirt; she lost a shoe. Not far from the ferry her body gave way, and she could walk no more. The child kissed her again and again, shouting for help; she too spent her last strength, calling out, call after call.
Help! Is anyone there? Save my mother!
The cry reached the ferry. The old ferryman came at the sound—without a word he lifted the fainting woman in his arms and strode toward the hut by the river.
Don't be afraid. The house is warm. Child, come.

Only then did the child see the old man who carried her: hair all white, a vest of coarse cloth, two arms hard as boat-timber. He wanted to cry and held it in fiercely, tiny fists clenched, running behind.

Inside, another old man was bent over, lighting the fire. At the sound of footsteps he raised his head—first a boy's face that seemed half-familiar, then the fainting woman in the old man's arms. The fire leapt. He knew her at a glance; and in that instant he knew who the child was.
The garden outside the great city, many years ago, rushed before his eyes. He dared not look again, dared not think. The wood in his hands fell to the floor with a crack.
Lay her… on my bed. Quickly.

The fire burned higher, lighting four faces: the fainting mother, the child with a wet, smeared face, the old man who had carried her, and the old man at the fire, still standing, his hands faintly trembling. Outside the window the river ran on, sound after sound, knowing nothing of this, intent only on the sea.

cards.title: Death at the Ferry

segments.text: The wound was washed, yet it had already blackened, and the whole arm was swollen. After the herbs, she slowly opened her eyes. She lay on his bed; he bent over her. She thought she was still dreaming, and smiled, gazing at that face. In the doorway the child she had brought was crying, out of breath.

You have grown old, my dear; your hair is white. Yet you remind me of that young Samana who once stood outside my garden—barefoot, covered in dust, with an honest gaze. You now are more like him than you were when you left the city. You have a Samana's eyes again. Ah—just now… did you still know me?
I knew you at a glance.
Her gaze turned to the {{e_xiaoxiduo|Siddhartha's son}} beside the bed, and she signed him to come near.
Look at him well. He is your son.

Her gaze grew distant; she closed her eyes. The child began to cry. He lifted the boy onto his knee, stroked his hair, and in a singing tone slowly recited a prayer learned in childhood. Those distant words came back, one by one. The child grew quiet, and sobbed himself to sleep.

By the stove the ferryman was cooking rice, his head down. He looked up at the woman on the bed, then at his friend, and smiled a helpless smile—both knew the herbs could keep her only a little while.
She is dying.
The ferryman nodded; the fire lit his kind face. The smell of rice mixed with the smell of medicine and spread through the hut.
When she woke again, her face was full of pain. He watched her quietly, intently, waiting, sharing her pain. She felt it, and her eyes found his.
Your gaze is wholly different from before… tell me, have you found it—found peace in the heart?
He smiled and gently stroked her hand.
You have found it. I can see it. …I shall have peace too.
You have it already.

She had meant to go and see the dying {{e_qiaodamo|Gotama}}—that awakened saint—to look once upon his peace; yet in the end she had found only her old lover. She felt that this too was good, as good as seeing the other. She wanted to tell him so, but her lips would no longer obey; she only looked at him in silence.
He watched life recede slowly from her eyes. When the last tremor passed over her body, he reached out and gently closed them.
He gathered the white hair scattered on the pillow, and tucked in the quilt, as if she might take cold.

He sat a long time, looking at her old, weary face, at the shrunken lips. He remembered how, many years ago, he had compared her mouth to a newly picked fig. In the same instant he seemed to see two young faces—red mouths, eager eyes—as if all of them were alive in this moment.

That night he did not eat. He sat alone outside the door and listened to the river all night. The river counselled him in nothing; it only flowed, as if to say: life is like a river—some come, some go.

Before sunrise the two old men built a pyre on the {{e_huozangqiu|burial mound}}—the ferryman's dead wife had been burned here many years before. The child still slept, his brow still furrowed. When the fire rose, he looked at the river and took the old man's hand.

cards.title: Broken Bowls

segments.text: On the day of the funeral the child cried as if his heart would tear. After that he did not cry. For days he sat pale on the burial mound, staring into the distance, his heart locked, struggling before his fate. The man who called himself his father respected the grief and did not press him, left him be. He honoured the child's sorrow: the boy did not yet know him, and could not love him as a father.

The father knew well: this eight-year-old had been spoiled from infancy by {{e_jiamola|Kamala}}. In the city house he had been used to fine food, soft beds, servants at a lifted hand. How could such a one settle at once in a poor hut? So the father did not hurry, did not scold; he only did many things for the child in silence: made the bed, mended clothes, kept the best portion of every meal for him.

But the child's heart did not soften at all. Coarse rice was set down; he tasted it and pushed it away, saying it was not food for a human being; asked to help with a little work, he turned his head aside; the fruit trees the other old man grew behind the hut he stripped bare, green and red fruit flung on the ground. He hated the water for being bitter, the bed for being hard, the night for its mosquitoes, and had 'home' on his lips all day. One evening, over a trifle, he seized the two rice-bowls on the table and smashed them on the floor.
I won't eat this! This is not food for people! I want to go home—back to my own house in the city! Even the water there is sweet!
Very well. If you don't care for it, leave it. I have left you a mango, on the window-ledge.
Who wants your mango! Stop pretending—I hate that good man's face of yours most of all!

The bowls were broken. The father crouched, picked up the shards one by one, swept them clean, and as usual warmed the rice again, saying nothing. His heart was not without bitterness: for months he had waited for his son to understand him, to take his love, even a little in return. He came to see that this child brought him not joy but trouble. Yet he would rather have the trouble than the ease of having no child.

The child, for his part, hoped more that he would lose his temper. A scolding, a blow even? But this father answered every rudeness with a smile, every wilfulness with kindness—and in the child's eyes that was the most hateful cunning, the trick of an old fox.

From then on the two old men divided the work: the {{e_weisudewa|Vasudeva}} took all the ferry's labour on himself, and the father kept the hut and the child. The child grew bolder. He had long noticed: the coppers and silver the passengers paid were kept in a bark {{e_shuangselan|two-coloured basket}} hung at the bow, and no one watched anyone. The child's gaze rested on that basket a long time; he said nothing.
That night the old ferryman drew his friend outside. The smile was gone from his wrinkles.
Friend. Tonight we must talk.

The father looked at the old man's face in the moonlight, and his heart sank. He half knew what would be said—the words he most feared to hear, and could least escape. The river ran at their feet, sound after sound, as if urging him to answer.

cards.title: Broken Oars

segments.text: The evening before, the powder that had gathered for months in the hut at last went off. The father told the child to gather sticks in the woods for the evening fire. The boy stood still, stamped both feet, fists clenched, and roared out all his contempt in his father's face.

Gather your own sticks! I am not your servant! I know you dare not beat me—you only punish me with your piety and your patience! You want me to be like you? Never! I hate you—I would rather be a thief, rather go to hell, than be like you!
The father stood as if struck on the head. He opened his mouth; nothing came.

The father had been waiting patiently all along, hoping his son would in the end understand him, would accept his love, would even repay it. Yet the father began to realise that his son had brought him not the slightest joy or peace, but only added to his troubles and sorrow.

The child rushed out, and did not come back till late at night; he fell asleep without a word. The father sat in the dark half the night, those hard words still buzzing in his ears, like a blow in the face. Next morning the bed was empty. The boy was gone.

The {{e_shuangselan|two-coloured basket}} hung at the bow was gone too—bark-woven, holding the passengers' coppers and silver. The {{e_duchuan|ferry}} at the bank was gone as well. The quilt on the bed was folded neatly. The father ran to the river in one breath, and far off saw the empty boat moored on the far shore. He understood it all.
I must follow him! A child cannot cross this forest alone; he will come to harm. We will bind a raft and cross at once!

A raft we must bind—the boat has to be brought back. But friend, let him go. He is no longer a child; he knows how to look after himself. He is finding the road back to the city. He is right; do not forget that: he is walking his own road, and no one can stop him.
His own road? He is only eight! He will lose his way, go hungry, meet bad men—how can you ask me to let go?
And if you catch him, what then? Bind him and bring him back in the boat?
At least he would be alive! At least he would not be among wolves!
I can see you are suffering. Yet all this suffering springs from blind attachment. Before long you will laugh at it yourself.

The father answered no more. He swung an axe at the bamboo; sweat ran down his temples; blisters rose on his palms and he did not stop. The old man helped him bind the poles tight with grass-rope. The raft went in, and the current drove it far downstream; they poled hard against the stream, and at last reached the other shore.
Why do you… carry an axe with you?
Perhaps our {{e_chuanjiang|oar}} are already gone.

So it was. The empty boat's bottom was clean; nothing was left. Before he fled, the child had broken the oars and thrown them in the river—so the men could not row after him. A hard mind, and a thorough one. The old man pointed at the empty bottom and smiled, saying nothing—the smile said plainly: Do you still not see? Your son does not wish to be pursued. He crouched and began, in silence, to shape a new oar. The father looked into the depths of the woods, clenched his fists, and walked quickly in.

There were small footprints in the woods, leading toward the great city. The old man looked at the prints, then at his friend's ashen face, and swallowed the words at his lips. The sun stood overhead, white and glaring; the two walked one behind the other, and neither spoke again.

cards.title: Ten Thousand Sounds Become Om

segments.text: After the son left, the wound still ached dully. Seeing other travellers cross with their children, he felt, to his own surprise, a jealousy: in this world even bad men have children with them—why not I? One day he could not bear it; he poled the {{e_duchuan|ferry}} to the other shore, meaning to search the city once more.

In the dry season the river was clear and shallow, yet strangely loud. The river was laughing—plainly, mocking this old man. He stopped, bent to look at the reflection, and suddenly knew the face: it was like his own father's. In those days he too had forced his father to let him leave home, and never returned. What his father had swallowed alone was what he now swallowed. Had his father not suffered the very same pain he now suffered at the loss of a son? This meaningless repetition was a circle drawn by fate.
He poled back, his heart bitter and confused; more than once he wanted to laugh aloud at himself. Yet he had one last road: to confess to the old man, to tell everything.

In the hut the old man was weaving a basket. His eyes were dim, his hands slow, yet the peace on his face was as it had always been. He sat down beside him and slowly poured out everything within: the longing to search in the city, the river's mockery, the guilt toward his father, the thoughts he was ashamed even to admit to himself.

The old man listened in silence. As he spoke he suddenly felt something was wrong: his trouble flowed into the old man's heart and came back cool and clear. Was this still a man? This motionless listener was plainly a great tree catching the rain, was plainly the river itself.
He had finished. The old man looked at him, worn, said nothing, took his hand, and led him to sit by the river.
You have heard its mockery. But you have not yet heard everything. Come, let us listen again.
The two old men sat in silence, listening to the river sing.
Do you hear?
He nodded.
Listen further!

He listened more deeply. Many images rose on the water: his father, alone in grief for a lost son; himself, alone in longing for the child who had fled; his son, alone on a road of burning desire. The three generations flowed into one river. Each clung to his goal, each was bound by his goal, each suffered. The water was full of thirst, sting, and pursuit. The river ran toward its goal; one goal reached, another rose, never ceasing.

He no longer told which sound was weeping, which was laughter. Joy and sorrow, good and evil, a mother's song and a dying groan—ten thousand voices wound together into one great song. And when his heart no longer seized any one of them, only a single syllable remained in that song—{{e_om|Om}}. The syllable a Brahmin's child could chant from the first memory, meaning: perfection. Ten thousand sounds become one; the one is all.

The old man turned and smiled. The smile unfolded from every wrinkle, radiant. In the same moment the same smile rose on his own face. His wound began to close; the pain sank like a stone to the river-bed. From that moment he no longer fought his fate.

cards.title: The Last Bow

segments.text: At dawn the old monk was to go on. At the hut door, after much hesitation, he asked a last question. He was one of the strictest in keeping the precepts in the {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—those who wore yellow robes, begged with bowls, wandered the four directions, and spent their lives preaching the teaching.
Friend, before I go on, tell me: have you some creed, some learning, that upholds your life?

You know well that from youth I have doubted every creed. Yet there is one thing I have found, and I can tell you: wisdom cannot be spoken. Knowledge can be taught; wisdom cannot. The wisdom a wise man tries to tell another always sounds foolish.
You are speaking strangely again… what does that mean?

The opposite of every truth is also true. Words can say only half—like parting the river with a hand; in a moment it is one river again. I think only one thing truly matters: to love this world. Not to despise it—whether sin or piety, wisdom or folly, all is necessary. Not to hate it or resist it, nor to hate ourselves; to look upon it and all life with love, with wonder, with reverence.

The old monk was silent. The words were strange and hard. Yet this man's every gesture, his eyes, his brow, his smile, held a purity and a peace—a radiance he had seen in only one other: the Blessed One who had already entered Nirvana. Nirvana is the stillness beyond birth and death.

A comparison even crossed his mind: the Blessed One's teaching was clear, definite, never so odd as this; yet this man's gaze and hands gave off a holiness he had not seen since the Blessed One's passing. The old monk's heart was in turmoil; already leaving, he turned back and bowed with deep feeling.

We are both old; we may not meet again in this life. Friend, I can see you have found peace; I have not. Tell me a little more—something I can carry in my breast upon the road. My road is often hard and dark.
He looked at the old monk in silence, with a calm, peaceful smile. Then he spoke softly.
Bend closer. Nearer still. Kiss my forehead.
The old monk was greatly astonished, yet a strong love and obedience pushed him; he bent and touched the forehead lightly with his lips. In that instant a miracle occurred.

He no longer saw his friend's face. He saw a thousand forms arising and passing: a dying fish with its mouth wide, a newborn infant red in the face; a murderer raising a knife, a sinner on his knees; men and women in an embrace, the stiff dead; wild boar, crocodile, bull, birds… ten thousand forms turning, loving one another and destroying one another, endlessly changing, endlessly reborn. He seemed to hear again the great song by the river, ten thousand voices singing only one word: {{e_om|Om}}.

And over it all lay a thin, transparent smile—peaceful, subtle, hovering above ten thousand births and deaths. The old monk knew it: it was the smile of the Blessed One, which he had revered and gazed upon all his life.

The old monk wept without restraint. Before the man who sat unmoving he bowed, deeply, deeply, to the ground. That peaceful smile called up all he had loved in his life, all that had been precious and holy.

cards.title: Newborn Infant

segments.text: I woke. I lay under {{e_yezishu|palm shore}}, the river running before my eyes, sunlight broken on the water. A river-wind made me shiver, yet I wanted to laugh. I do not remember how long I slept—as if a lifetime, and as if only an instant.

Yesterday I had meant to sink myself in this river. The rich man's sickness had eaten me hollow: fine clothes, dice, wine-feasts; twenty years I had turned round and round in {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—the cycle men call the turning of life between birth and death—and the longer I turned, the more numb the heart. I was sick of myself; even a glance at my reflection in the water made me retch.

Yet in the instant I let go, a syllable that had slept many years woke in the heart—{{e_om|Om}}. The first word a Brahmin's child can chant from memory, meaning 'perfection'. It sounded so lightly, as if someone under the water had called my name. I saw all at once how foolish I had been, sank down under the tree, and slept a deep sleep. That sleep had no dreams.

Now I have nothing: no property, no fine clothes, no place that will wait for me. Yet my heart is light as a newborn infant's; all things look new. So a man must taste his own foolishness and sin with his own hands, let them rot, let them die, before he can become a child again. The songbird in my breast was not dead—it had only been mute many years.
The river is singing. I will stay, stay beside it, ask it to teach me, and listen to what it tells. My old life has died on the other shore; the new life begins with this river.

cards.title: Year upon Year

segments.text: On the river one day was like the next, one year like the last. I rowed the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}, planted rice, wove baskets, and at dark ate with the old man. To others this white-haired ferryman had perhaps belonged to the river from birth.

So it seemed. Yet in my heart a ledger still ran, year after year. I had counted: in the city I wasted twenty years. That number twenty I still cannot wipe away—when I wake at night, the first thing I do is take it out and reckon it again.

Some passengers make me uneasy. A merchant in splendid clothes steps aboard, and I remember how I once stepped onto another man's boat just so; a loving young couple crosses, and I have to turn my face to the water. The old man never asks; he only shifts the pole a little toward me.

The most stifling are another kind: a white-haired old man helped aboard by his son. I set a stool for them, take the fare, pole to the other shore, watch them walk slowly away. Only when they are far do I dare think of it—the year I left home I walked so sure of myself, and never went back once. In which year my father ceased to be, I have never even asked a soul.

{{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—I used to speak of it fluently: men trapped, turning between birth and death, circle after circle. I do not speak of it now. I lack no doctrine, not a line; I only know that some accounts the river cannot wipe out for me in a day. It runs past my feet each day, making no sound, as if to say: slowly.

cards.title: He Has Her Eyes

segments.text: Firelight falls on {{e_dukoucaoshe|hut at the ferry}}, and on the mother and child on the bed. The child has cried himself to sleep on my knee; his mother lies there, the poison still in her wound.
I look at that small face again and again. Eight years old, silk clothes, a spoiled look—yet the way he knits his brow is plainly {{e_jiamola|Kamala}} when she was young. He has her eyes.

When I left the great city I did not know she already carried my child. {{e_xiaoxiduo|Siddhartha's son}} has grown till now in wealth: fine food, soft beds, servants at his call; and I, his father, was yesterday still rowing for a copper's fare.

I had thought myself different: the world was children, I was the one awake; I could not love, and need not. Now a son lies on my lap. So I too cannot escape—I too will worry, will fear, will want to press the world's best things on a child who loses his temper at me.

Will she rest in peace? She will. Before she went she saw the peace in my eyes, and said she would have it too. Very well; the rest of the road is mine: to raise this motherless child, day by day, year by year.

I owe her. When I was young I took her love as a lesson, learned it, and left, without looking back. Now she has given me a son—what have I to repay? Only to raise him, raise him upright, as she would have wished.
He will not acknowledge me; he hates this poor hut; it does not matter. I have patience enough—I will warm his heart, day by day, with kindness.

cards.title: A Night Listening to the River

segments.text: She is gone. Before dawn we must build a pyre for her on the {{e_huozangqiu|burial mound}}—the ferryman's dead wife was burned in the same place, many years ago. The child still sleeps, knowing nothing.
I did not sleep this night. The ferryman lay down in the goat-stall; I sat alone outside the hut and listened to the river all night.

Strange: fragments of my whole life rose tonight: the sacrificial fire in my father's house, hunger in the forest of austerities, the city's lamps and wine, the golden cage in her garden… they came without order, all at once, as the river does not divide source from sea, and all is only 'now'. Now I rose to hear the child's breathing at the door; now I sat and heard the water.
I remember she once said she wished to give her garden to the order. She did it. In her life she could take, and she could let go; I have spent a whole lifetime on the lesson of 'letting go'.
My friend said I had suffered, yet sorrow had not entered my heart. He asked why I did not grieve. Yes—why?
I was once rich, once happy; now that she is gone I am not poorer but richer—my son has come back to me. This is what she left me with her last breath.

The river sang all night. Near dawn I understood: it was not weeping for her; it was singing life itself—some come, some go, the river is still the river. I touched the child's hair and rose to carry the first bundle of wood.

cards.title: The Listener

segments.text: The night was deep. In this hut by the {{e_linzhongdukou|ferry in the woods}} the oil-lamp was nearly spent; the river's sound came in at the window. The guest had just told the half of his life, and suddenly felt that this night's telling had been more easing than twenty years of thought.

I thank you. And I have one more thing to thank you for—you know so well how to listen. Very few know the art of listening; I have walked most of my life and never met a listener like you. In this I would learn from you.
It is not hard. But you need not learn it from me.
From whom, then?
The river. The river taught me to listen. You will learn it from the river too. The river knows everything; a man can learn everything from it.
The river… what can it teach?

You have already learned one thing: to go downward, to sink, to seek the deepest ground. You who were rich and honoured are now an oarsman on the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}—that is going downward. Later you will learn another thing.
What other thing?

It is too late; we should sleep. I cannot tell you—you will find it yourself, perhaps you already know. I am not a learned man; I cannot speak, and I cannot think. I only know how to listen, how to honour. If I could speak, I should long ago have been a teacher. I am only a ferryman; my work is to take people across.
To take people across… thousands have gone over in your boat; do they all listen to the river as you do?

No. To thousands of travellers this river is only an obstacle on the road. They hurry for trade, for money, to wedding-feasts, on long journeys, turning in {{e_lunhui|Samsara}}—life circling between birth and death; men call it Samsara. The river blocks their way; the ferryman's work is to take them over quickly.
Are there no exceptions?

There are. Among thousands, a few dozen, perhaps only four or five—to them the river is not an obstacle. They can hear it speak, and will listen with the heart. To them the river becomes a holy thing, as it is to me.
I should like to be one of those four or five.
You will. Sleep, my friend. The river is outside the window; it is not in haste to teach you, and you need not be in haste to learn.
The lamp went out. Listening to the water beyond the window, he felt for the first time that 'listening' too was a craft—a harder craft than rowing.

cards.title: Before the Garden Gate

segments.text: I followed all the way to the city's edge. I did not find my son, yet I stopped before a garden gate—{{e_mingjihuayuan|courtesan's garden}} I knew. Decades ago it had been the most beautiful place in the city, belonging to a {{e_mingji|courtesan}}—courtesans then were independent women of wealth and art, who chose their own lovers. Now the garden has been given to the order; yellow-robed monks come and go in the shade.

I stood a long time. The past rose scene by scene: a young Samana with long hair standing outside the garden, covered in dust, seeing her in the palanquin for the first time; the kiss under the pavilion; later the fine clothes, the counting-house, the dice, the songbird in the golden cage… my whole life, it seemed, was written on the road before me.

Yet what have I come here to do? To pursue my son. And if I catch him? Drag him back to the hut he hates? Standing at the garden gate I suddenly saw how foolish the thought was: I cannot help him. I cannot force my own way of living upon his head.

I love him; the love is like a wound, and it still hurts. But a wound should not rot in the heart; it should slowly close. He came into the world to walk his own road, and I too should go back to my river.

At the garden gate a monk set two bananas before me. Only then did I feel the thick dust in my hair, and I did not know how many hours I had stood there. I smiled at him, picked up the bananas, turned, and walked toward the ferry. The river and my friend were still waiting for me.

cards.title: Send Him Back to the City

segments.text: That night, when the shards of the bowls had been swept away and the child was asleep, the old man drew his friend outside and sat on the log by the river. He said more this evening than in the whole past year.
Forgive me. As a friend I must speak with you. I know you are anxious, and much troubled. Truthfully, {{e_xiaoxiduo|Siddhartha's son}} troubles you greatly—and me as well.
He is still a child. He has just lost his mother.

That little bird is used to another life, another nest. He did not flee wealth in disgust, as you once did; he was dragged from that nest. I have asked the river many times; the river laughed, laughed at the foolishness you and I have done. Water returns to water; the young remain young. Your son will not be happy here. He too has a road of his own to walk.

How can I part from him? Give me more time. I am fighting for him; I want to enter his heart. I will win him with love and patience. One day the river will speak to him too—the river is calling him as well.

Of course the river is calling him too. But do you and I know to which road he will be led? His heart is proud and hard; he will suffer much, and err much. Tell me: do you discipline him? Is he obedient to you? Have you beaten him, punished him?
No. I cannot do those things.

I know. You do not blame him, do not punish, do not command—you know gentleness is better than severity, kindness better than force. Yet friend, might this not be another error of yours? Are you not binding him with love? Day after day, with your goodness and patience, making him more ashamed? How can you keep a proud child in this hut, to live with two old men of the hills? Is that not a punishment for him?
What do you think… I should do?

Send him back to the city. Send him to his mother's house—{{e_mingjihuayuan|courtesan's garden}} has been given away, but there are still servants in the house. Give him to the servants, to teachers; let him meet other boys and girls; let him live in the world that is his. Have you truly never thought this?

You can see through my heart. I think it often. And yet—how is a boy like him to stand in the world? He will surely think himself above others, lose himself in pleasure and power, and walk his father's road again.

Ask the river, my friend! Do you truly think keeping him at your side can protect him? What father, what teacher, can stop a man from living his own life? Who protected that young Samana in those days? His father's piety, his teachers' precepts—none of it could stop him. Even if you died ten times for your son, you could not alter his fate by a hair.

The old man had never spoken so many words in one breath. His friend thanked him kindly, went back to the hut with his head down, and could not close his eyes all night. All those reasons he had thought, all he understood—but stronger than reason was love. He had never loved anyone so wholly, so blindly, so painfully.
Give me more time. I cannot.
Outside, the old man looked at the river and sighed softly. From that day both began a silent endurance—one enduring a son, the other a friend.

cards.title: Farewell, River

segments.text: After that dusk of listening to the river, the hurt in his friend's heart at last faded. Life at the ferry went on: rowing, taking fares, mending the raft. Only the old man more and more often laid down his work and gazed into the woods. A few days later he stood up on the bank and looked a long time into his friend's eyes—eyes that held the same peace as his own.
I have been waiting for this moment, my friend. Now that it has come, I may go.
You are going? Where?
Into the woods, into the unity of all things. For a long time I have been the ferryman of this crossing; now it is finished. The {{e_duchuan|ferry}} is yours, the ferry is yours.
If you go, what of the ferry? What of the travellers?
The ferry has you. You are already a ferryman—a better one than I. The hut I leave you too: rice in the jar, the net on the beam, the oars behind the door.
I will look after them, and after every one who crosses.
But I have so much still unlearned—the river's ten thousand sounds becoming one, and I have only just heard that word…

You have already heard {{e_om|Om}}—the one into which ten thousand voices flow, the sound of perfection. He who has heard it needs no teacher. The river itself will teach you, as it once taught me, sentence by sentence, never weary.
In the days to come, whom shall I learn from?
Learn from the river. All I have I learned from it. It has more patience than I, and more honesty.
That year you ferried me across and took nothing. I have not yet repaid you.
You stayed and became my apprentice, and kept me company all these years. That is the repayment.
Then shall we… meet again?
Do not be sad. Look at the river—it bids farewell to every wavelet, and never turns back.
I am not sad. I am… unwilling to let go.
If you cannot let go, ferry it to the other shore. Ferry others, and ferry yourself. —Farewell, my hut. Farewell, my river. Farewell, my friend.
I understand. Go. Thank you—thank you for teaching me to listen.
I will see you to the edge of the woods.
No need. A ferryman does not see a ferryman off. Keep your ferry well.

He bowed deeply to the man about to leave. The old man turned into the woods, his step peaceful, his face as if it shone. That night he sat alone on the log and listened to the river the whole night through—among ten thousand sounds, what he heard was no longer farewell, but perfection.

cards.title: Seeking and Finding

segments.text: The ferry was short one ferryman, yet the days went on. One day an old monk came to the crossing. He was of the {{e_sengtuan|Gotama's order}}—those in yellow robes who begged with bowls and wandered the four directions preaching the teaching. He had heard it said that a saintly ferryman lived by this river, and came out of his way to see him. He had kept the precepts all his life, yet his heart was never at peace—he felt he had not yet found the final thing.
Old man, please ferry me across.
At the other shore the old monk was in no haste to go; he only studied the old man who poled.
You have ferried so many pilgrims and monks, and never tired. I have heard of your great peace and your gift of listening. Are you—perhaps—a seeker yourself?
Venerable sir, you are already old, and you wear the robe of a disciple of {{e_qiaodamo|Gotama}}. Do you still call yourself a seeker?
I am old, it is true. But I have never ceased seeking, and I never shall—it seems to be my fate. You too, I think, have sought. Friend, can you give me some guidance?
What I can say may be of little worth. And yet—perhaps you have sought too much, and so cannot find.
What does that mean?

When a man is seeking, his eyes see only what he seeks. Bound to the goal, he discovers nothing, obtains nothing. Seeking means having a goal; finding means freedom, openness, the laying down of every goal. Venerable one, you may well be a seeker—you pursue so hard that you cannot see what is before you.
I still do not understand. You mean…?
Venerable one, many years ago you came to this river and found a man asleep. You sat beside him and watched over his sleep—yet you did not know the sleeper, [[NPC2]].
The old monk stood as if struck by lightning, staring hard at the ferryman.
Is it you? …Is it really you? How is it that this time, still, I did not know you. My old friend! You have changed—you are a ferryman now?
Yes, I have become a ferryman. Men change, put on one garment and then another; so have I. You are welcome. Tonight, stay in my hut.
Good! I have a bellyful of questions for you; tonight I shall not sleep, I fear.
Ask. The night is long, and the river does not sleep.
Then tell me of yourself first—how did you come to be a ferryman?
That night the old monk slept in the bed the other ferryman had left empty. The heaviest question in his heart he kept for the next morning.

cards.title: The Seventeenth Boat on the Mound

segments.text: {{e_jiamola|Kamala}} said we should be gone only a few days. She said a very great man outside the city was about to die; she wanted to see him once, and we should be back in time for the rains. She told me to wear my strongest shoes. I would not walk; I wanted a palanquin; she said we could not take a palanquin this time.

The thing in the grass I saw first. Grey, short, like a bit of broken rope. I opened my mouth and did not shout. But within a few seconds she had already cried out and was sitting on the ground. I have told this to no one. I think it over and over: what if I had shouted sooner?

They carried her into a hut. It smelled of fish; the floor was earth, the bowls were broken. Before dawn she did not speak any more. The next day they stacked wood on the {{e_huozangqiu|burial mound}} by the water, stacked it very neatly, as if for one of their own.

I sat on the mound and counted the boats that passed on the river. Seventeen the first day, nine the second. They brought food; I would not eat; they brought it a second time, and I still would not. Hunger hurts, but if I eat it is as if I have given in. The wind blew ash onto my legs; I did not brush it off.

Neither of them hurried me. One only sat far off braiding rope; the other came and went, setting a bowl of water where I could reach it. The more they did this, the more I understood: they did not mean to send me away.

The white-haired man says he is my father. But I have no father. I have a house with walls around it, a gardener who picks fruit for me, a bird that could copy speech. As soon as I know the way back to the city, I shall go at once.

cards.title: The River Would Not Carry Him

segments.text: In the afternoon no one crossed. [[NPC1]] untied the rope, jumped onto the {{e_duchuan|ferry}}, and rammed the pole into the water as the grown men did. The bow swung, and the boat drifted sideways downstream. The old man [[NPC2]] on the bank watched, neither shouting nor running.
Stop staring! Come and give me a push!
I cannot. The water runs down; the more you fight, the farther it takes you. Take in the pole, and wait for it to come in of itself.

The boat turned twice in a bend and struck a stand of reeds and stopped. The old man rolled up his trousers, went in, held the boat with one hand and lifted the child ashore with the other. The child flung off his hand, shaking all over—whether from cold or from anger, he could not have said.
This boat is bad.
The boat is good. You were missing one thing in your hands—you used a pole, and the river is so deep the pole cannot reach the bottom.
Then you take me. I will pay.
Pay?

That {{e_shuangselan|two-coloured basket}} hung at the bow is full of the coppers people give for the crossing. I have counted; it is enough. I will pay double—take me back to the city, to the street with the stone lions; I know my own door.
That is not my money.
The basket hangs on your boat.
The basket hangs on my boat; the money was given to this river by others, and I only keep it for the river. I cannot spend it for the river today.
You two old things, one playing deaf, one playing stupid.
The old man was not angry. He wrung out his wet trousers, crouched, fished a long wooden thing from the boat's bottom, laid it across his knees, and wiped it slowly with a cloth.
Why don't you beat me? He doesn't beat me because he dares not, I suppose. And you?

There is no bond between us; if I beat you, you would have a ready reason to hate me. As it is, if you hate me you must invent a reason yourself—inventing reasons is tiring, and when you are tired you think of other things.
I am not tired.
Mm. When I was young I was not tired either.
If my mother were still here, one word would have bought your boat.
If she were still here, there would be no need to buy. When she asked, I ferried.

The child waited for the next sentence; the old man said no more. He held out the long thing in his hands and showed him how to grip with both hands, how to use the waist. The child turned his head, as if too lazy to learn. Yet he remembered every word: without this one thing, the boat goes nowhere.

cards.title: The Thing Thrown into the Water

segments.text: Yesterday at dusk I roared out all the words I had saved for months. Then I ran, and sat in the woods till midnight. When I came back a lamp was still left in the house, and a mango on the window-ledge. I did not touch it.

I waited till they slept. The two old men slept deeply, their breathing long and short, like two ropes wrongly tied. I felt my way to the bow, took down the {{e_shuangselan|two-coloured basket}}, crouched in the moonlight and counted the coppers one by one into my pocket—enough to last a few days in the city and find my own door.

Crossing was easier than I had thought. Hands low, waist turning: the old man who always played the fool had taught me that himself. In the middle the water pushed hard; I clenched my teeth and poled through, shoes wet to the ankles. On the other shore I tied the boat, then untied it; thought, and in the end tied it again.

Then I did one thing: with all my strength I broke every {{e_chuanjiang|oar}} in the boat and threw them all into the water. Not because I feared he would follow—if he meant to, he could bind a raft and still catch me. I wanted him to spend himself for me once, to sweat, to curse an ugly word or two. In all my life I have never heard him curse anyone, not once. I am sick of that smile he always wears.

A little white was just showing on the horizon when I took the road to the great city. Far on I looked back once: a point of lamp still burned by the hut. He will probably come looking for me, but he will not beat me—that I have always known.
