pages.title: A Farewell Stood Through the Night

segments.text: In ancient India twenty-five hundred years ago, a man's station was fixed at birth; the highest rank was called Brahmin—hereditary priest-nobles. Siddhartha, raised in this house of mango trees, could recite all the scriptures, perform the whole rite of bathing and sacrifice, and argue with a sharp tongue. Everyone in the town loved him; his friend Govinda honoured him above all others, and was content to be his shadow.

Yet he was not happy. Father and teachers poured wisdom into his vessel, and the vessel was never full; bathing could wash the dust from the body, not the trouble from the heart; the sacrificial fire, however beautiful, could not reach the source he sought. The scriptures said there was an eternal, undying Atman in the depths of the heart—and that road his father could not walk for him, nor his teachers, nor the sacred verses.

So in the deep of night he went into his father's room and asked leave to go and become a Samana—an ascetic who leaves the family and walks naked in austerity. The father was displeased and went back to sleep; the son stood where he was, hands folded, unmoving. Three times in the night the old man rose, and from a small window saw that still figure in the moonlight; anger, anxiety, and fear turned little by little into understanding: this son could no longer be kept.

At first light the father put out his hand and gently touched his shoulder: Go, into the forest; if you find the bliss of heaven, come back and teach me. The young man tried to step; his body swayed—he had stood in that place a whole night. The legs might tremble; the heart must not.
I will stand till dawn, till noon, till night—until he himself gives me leave to go.

At the next daybreak he left the still-sleeping town alone. At the last hut on the town's edge a crouched figure slipped from the shadows and followed in silence: Govinda had not slept; he had already decided—wherever you go, I will go, as your companion, your servant, your shadow.

pages.title: The Narcotic, and Rumours of the Awakened One

segments.text: The years in the forest were counted in hunger. One meal a day, a fast of fourteen days, then of twenty-eight; standing in the heat, standing in the rain, lying in thorns. In meditation his soul left the body, became a hawk over the bamboo, a rotting jackal on the sand—yet each time he woke again in sun and moonlight, and was himself again. The elders praised him as the fiercest in practice, the quickest to learn; in his heart he quietly doubted what it all meant.

After three years he admitted to himself: meditation, breath, fasting, were only narcotics for fleeing the self. A herdsman drinking a few bowls of rice-wine in a tavern, sinking into sleep, was fleeing in the same way; drown the self a hundred times, and on waking it still sat waiting in its place.
The place he reaches with one bowl of wine, we need a month of hunger and a month of sitting to reach.

On the alms-road he said heavier words to Govinda: the eldest is sixty and has not attained Nirvana; you and I will grow old the same way, and fall equally short—we are only going in circles; perhaps learning itself is Atman's greatest enemy. Govinda still believed the path was a rising spiral; yet watching that back that was always half a step ahead, he felt panic for the first time: this man, he would soon not be able to follow.

Just then rumours poured into the jungle: a sage of the Sakya clan had appeared, had conquered the world's sufferings, stilled the wheel of rebirth; people called him the Awakened One. Some praised, some mocked. And the subject of the rumours was at that moment silently begging in the lanes of Savathi—in his view, rumours themselves grow old and lose their teeth; what mattered was that those who slept under the trees this year were twice last year's number.

The two young men asked leave to quit the jungle and hear the teaching with their own ears; the eldest flew into a rage. Siddhartha came near the old man and gazed into his eyes with complete attention—the very art the old man had taught, year by year, with his own hands—and the old man suddenly fell silent, bowed, and stammered a blessing. The morning mist broke; the two set out empty-handed toward the rumoured city.

pages.title: After the Teaching, Each His Own Road

segments.text: Asking along the way, the two young Samanas entered Savathi and spent the night in a garden monastery a rich elder had given to the Buddha. At dawn, among hundreds of monks in the same dress, Siddhartha knew that man at a glance: yellow robe, alms-bowl, no pride in him; face, gait, even every finger showed perfection, and his smile was no different from an infant's. He spoke not a word; merely walking so quietly, he was known.

Before the evening teaching, the Buddha told an old monk to prepare one more robe: the shy come earliest and stand last; when I entered the garden I saw one who had already stood a long while. Indeed, when the teaching ended, Govinda, always shy, pressed forward, his voice tight but without hesitation, and asked to take refuge. He was received.

That night the two friends walked long in the woods, lay down, and long could not sleep. One wept; the other only blessed him again and again: you have always followed me a step behind; now at last you have taken a step of your own; may you go on by this road, may you find salvation. At the next dawn the old monks gave out yellow robes; Govinda put one on and embraced the friend of his youth—from then he stayed, and was no one's shadow.

Siddhartha, the next day, spoke plainly to the Buddha's face: Your teaching is unified, crystal-clear, yet there is a small crack—the experience you yourself attained cannot be given in words, and so no one can be saved by doctrine; I will leave all creeds and teachers, and go on by my own road. The Buddha listened in silence, eyes lowered, with a faint smile.
You are clever, Samana from afar; you know how to argue with skill. My friend—beware your own excess of cleverness.

Leaving the garden, Siddhartha woke as from a long dream: he had meant to destroy the self and find Atman in the ruins, and had for that very reason lost himself all along the way. From today everything was reversed—learn from the self, take the self as teacher. He looked about: the world was gold, deep blue, green, strangely beautiful; meaning was not behind things, but in the things themselves.
The Buddha watched that light-footed figure go out the garden gate. The missing corner, perhaps, was a door left for such a man.

pages.title: Across the River, a First Sight Outside the Garden

segments.text: Leaving the Buddha's garden, Siddhartha travelled alone several days, his heart light and bright: the world had suddenly become so beautiful—gold, deep blue, green—it had been there all along. At evening he came to a great river and lodged in the hut at the ferry; the ferryman shared bread, water, and mangoes, and at dawn poled him across. On the far shore he could not find a copper; the ferryman only smiled.
I take no money from you. One day you will come and repay me. Water flows out and flows back; it always turns.

He took it for a joke, and entered the great city. By a beautiful unwalled garden outside the city he met a train of servants with gift-boxes, crowding round a fine palanquin; in it sat Kamala, the city's most famous courtesan, her small red mouth like a newly picked fig. As the palanquin passed he bowed deeply, and rising met those intelligent eyes—she nodded and smiled, then vanished into the garden.

The servants' eyes came like needles. For the first time he looked at himself in earnest: tangled long hair full of dust, a ragged loincloth barely covering him. In the forest he had been proud of poverty; at this garden gate he suddenly felt himself only a beggar. So he changed his skin: shaved, combed, put on hair-oil, bathed in the river; the rice-cake he had begged he threw to a dog—from today he was no longer a beggar.

In this city where everyone had money and everyone loved money, a man who had thrown everything away felt, for the first time in his life, a clear wanting: fine clothes, costly shoes, a bag full of coin—so that he might walk into that garden with dignity, and see those eyes again.

pages.title: A Poem for a Kiss, Letters for a Living

segments.text: The next day he waited, made new, at the garden entrance. In the pavilion Kamala named her terms: the young men who come to me all wear splendid clothes, costly shoes, scented hair, and bags full of money. What he offered in return were three arts she did not understand.
I can think, I can wait, I can fast.

He added an impromptu poem, and received a kiss—and in that kiss such rich learning: conquest, refusal, and temptation. She gave him a white robe and had a servant lead him out by winding paths. Only two days in the city, and he had already kissed the most beautiful woman in it.

She opened the next door for him as well: Kamaswami, the city's richest merchant, was expecting his visit. Her only charge—be friendly to him, but do not be a cringing servant; I want you as his equal, or I shall be displeased.

In the great house the merchant fired questions: You are in some difficulty, are you not? You have nothing; what can you give? He answered without hurry, the same answer: I can think, I can wait, I can fast; a man who can fast is not driven by hunger, and so can wait in peace. Given a contract to read, he missed not a word; asked to write, he took up the pen: Writing is beautiful, yet not so as thought; wit is beautiful, yet not so as patience. The merchant read it twice and at once kept him as a guest. The one being tested was unhurried; the one testing was the first to be moved.

From then servants brought clothes and shoes, and important letters and papers were put in his hands. He treated trade as a game: the rules he learned in earnest; winning and losing he did not take to heart. Kamaswami sighed to an old friend: When he gains, he smiles; when he loses, he smiles, and sleeps like a child just the same. Someone suggested giving him a third of the profit, to let money stick to him—yet he turned and gave the share to the labourers at the harbour; if he lost, he made it up himself without a word, and went off to someone else's wedding-feast.
The merchant rose at midnight to count the books; he slept like a child. There are such men in the world: everything in their hands, and nothing taken in earnest.

pages.title: The Fall, and the Death of a Songbird

segments.text: Those years Siddhartha lived a double life. At the appointed hour he went to Kamala in fine clothes and costly shoes, and from a child who knew nothing of love became her proudest pupil; in trade he remained an outsider—his master careful and anxious, sleepless three nights over a cargo, while he treated it as a game. Sent to a village for rice, he found the rice already bought; he was not angry, simply stayed, feasted the farmers, went to a wedding, and came back content.

One dusk after the lessons were done, Kamala named what they shared: You are the finest of all my lovers; one day I should like a child with you; yet you are still a Samana—you do not truly love me, you love no one. He admitted it: I am much like you; you too have no power to love. Ordinary people can love, like leaves rolling in the wind; they themselves are like stars, which the wind cannot reach, and which cannot reach the leaves' joy.
You do not truly love me—you love no one, is that not so?

Year by year the world seeped in like damp into a dying trunk. The wheel of abstinence, the wheel of thought, turned slower and slower; he learned to give orders, fine clothes and wine, and learned to gamble: thousands on a throw, and only when a great stake hung did he feel a little fear, sweet and terrible, and know he was still alive. Kamaswami was at first glad he would at last fret over money; later he could not smile—he did not love money, he hated it. The man in the mirror grew older and uglier by the day; the smiles grew fewer.

The height of the fall was a dream. On the last night Kamala asked him to tell the Buddha's story again, and said she wished to give her garden to the order; she held him, tears in her eyes, as if to wring a last drop of sweetness from this passing joy. That night he came home drunk, and at dawn dreamed the songbird in the golden cage stiff at the cage's floor—he started in terror, his heart wrung hard: as if all that was good and of worth in him had been thrown away with that dead bird.

He sat under the mango tree a whole day, reviewing his life from the start: had he left all those people only to become such a rich man as this? Night fell; he rose and said farewell to the tree, the garden, the city, and did not return. She was not surprised at the news; she only went to the golden cage, opened the little door, and let the bird go.

pages.title: A Word That Sounded by the Water

segments.text: Leaving the city, Siddhartha wandered into the woods and came to that same great river. That life he had tasted to the point of nausea; nothing in the world could comfort him. He held the great tree on the bank and looked down at the water; the cold in it mirrored the emptiness in his soul. He spat at his own reflection, let go, and gave himself to death—and in that instant a syllable that had slept twenty years sounded from the depths of the soul.
Om—the first word a Brahmin's child can chant from memory, meaning perfection.

The word sounded lightly; he saw all at once how foolish he had been, sank down under the tree, and fell into a deep, dreamless sleep. He had meant to drown in this river; and in truth that old, weary, despairing self had already drowned in it.

When he woke, a yellow-robed old monk was sitting before him, watching—a monk of the order, travelling, who had seen him sleep so deeply and stayed. Thanks, farewell—yet he smiled and spoke the other's name: Govinda. The old monk started: the most beloved friend of his youth, and he himself had twice failed to know him. He looked at this seeker in rich clothes, scented with perfume, bowed, and went on his way.

And in the city Kamaswami turned the ledger: not a coin touched, not a discrepancy. He would never accept the other explanation—that a man would lay down house, clothes, and trade, and for what? That room he left empty a whole year.

pages.title: Meeting Again at the Ferry, Year upon Year

segments.text: Many years later a white-haired old man in rich clothes came on foot, alone, to the ferry. The ferryman knew him: more than twenty years before he had ferried a young Samana across for nothing—today that word, you will come and repay me, was fulfilled. The old man would give his fine robes as fare, only asking to stay: a helper first, then an apprentice; I must learn to row. A smile rose from the depths of the ferryman's wrinkles: You are welcome; my name is Vasudeva.

That night the oil-lamp in the hut was nearly spent; the guest told his whole life the whole night through: birth, study, wealth, the fall, down to despair by the river and the waking. The ferryman only listened—did not interrupt, did not press, did not blame, did not praise; this night's telling was more easing than twenty years of thought. He asked to learn the art of listening; the ferryman said: You need not learn it from me—the river taught me to listen.

And waking from that sleep by the river, he was light as a newborn infant: so a man must taste his own foolishness and sin with his own hands, let them rot, let them die, before he can become a child again; the songbird in the breast was not dead, it had only been mute many years.

Life settled at the ferry: mending boats, shaping oars, planting rice, weaving baskets; he liked whatever he did, and learned quickly. At dusk after work the apprentice asked the master: Have you also learned this secret from the river—that time does not exist at all? The river is everywhere at once, and each place is only now; life too is a river; boy, man in his prime, old man, are only three stretches drawn by illusion.
What is spoken is leftover rice; what one tastes for oneself is the meal. So I do not speak. I only sit and listen with you.

The doctrine he understood; the ledger in his heart still ran, year after year: the twenty years wasted in the city, still reckoned when he woke at night. A white-haired old man helped aboard by his son; he set a stool for them—after leaving home he had never gone back; in which year his father ceased to be, he had never even asked.

Years ran past like the river. Travellers slowly noticed a strange thing: the smiles of the two ferrymen, old and younger, grew more and more alike—the same unfolding from a thousand fine lines, the same peace. Many, boarding, asked: Are you brothers? The two only looked at each other and smiled.

pages.title: Pilgrimage, Snakebite, Death at the Ferry

segments.text: Many more years passed; news that the Awakened One was dying ran like wildfire, and the ferry did not rest from dawn to dusk. In the stream of people walked a mother and child: the mother had once given her garden to the monks, and this time brought the child to see the saint on his last journey. Resting in the woods, a small snake darted from the grass—the child saw it first; he opened his mouth and did not shout.

The cry reached the ferry; the old ferryman lifted the fainting woman and went toward the hut. The other old man lighting the fire by the stove raised his head, knew her at a glance, and in that instant knew who the child was. He looked at that small face again and again: eight years old, the knitted brow plainly hers when she was young—he has her eyes. Only one road remained: to raise this motherless child, day by day.

The wound was washed, yet the herbs could keep her only a little while. Kamala woke and knew the man bending over her: You have grown old, your hair is white, yet you are more like that young Samana who once stood outside my garden than you were when you left the city. She had meant to see the Buddha a last time, and met her old lover first; she felt that this too was good, as good as seeing the other. When life receded slowly from her eyes, he reached out and gently closed them.

That night he did not eat; he sat alone outside the door and listened to the river all night: fragments of a whole life rose without order, as the river does not divide source from sea. At dawn the two old men built a pyre on the mound by the water—the ferryman's dead wife had been burned in the same place, many years before.

For days the child sat pale on the mound, counting the boats that passed: seventeen the first day, nine the second. The food they brought he would not eat—if he ate, it was as if he had given in. He had seen the snake first; this he told no one. The more they sat with him at a distance, the more he understood: they did not mean to send me away. The white-haired man says he is my father—I have no father.

pages.title: Two Broken Bowls, Flight with Broken Oars

segments.text: Many days after the funeral, the days still would not grow quiet. The child was spoiled; he tasted the coarse rice once and pushed it away; the fruit trees the old man had planted behind the hut were stripped bare; one evening, over a trifle, two rice-bowls smashed hard on the floor. The father crouched, picked up the shards one by one, swept them clean, and as usual warmed the rice again, saying nothing. The child hoped all the more that he would lose his temper—answering every rudeness with a smile was, in the child's eyes, the most hateful cunning. And the father would rather have the trouble than the ease of having no child.

The child again asked the old ferryman to take him back to the city, offering double fare—the coppers in the two-coloured basket at the bow he had already counted. The old man said, That is not my money; it is the river's; then laid an oar across his knees and showed him how to grip with both hands, how to use the waist. The child turned his head, pretending laziness, yet remembered every word: without this one thing, the boat goes nowhere.
Water returns to water; the young remain young. Are you not binding him with love? Send him back to the city.

That night the old ferryman drew his friend outside and said more than in the whole past year. The friend thanked him kindly, went back to the hut with his head down, and could not close his eyes all night. All those reasons he had thought, all he understood—but stronger than reason was love: he had never loved anyone so wholly, so blindly, so painfully.

The powder that had gathered for months at last went off one evening: the child roared out a bellyful of contempt in his father's face and rushed out; next morning the bed was empty, the two-coloured basket at the bow was gone, the ferry-boat was gone. The empty boat lay on the far shore; every oar had been broken and thrown into the river.
Not because I feared he would follow. I wanted him to spend himself for me once, to sweat, to curse an ugly word—in all my life I have never heard him curse anyone.

The two old men bound a raft and crossed; the father followed all the way to the city's edge, yet stopped at an old garden gate—decades ago he, long-haired, covered in dust, had stood here and seen her in the palanquin for the first time. He suddenly saw how foolish the thought was: he could not help his son, could not force his own way of living upon his son's fate. He picked up the two bananas a monk had set down, and turned back to the ferry.

pages.title: Ten Thousand Sounds Become Om, the Last Bow

segments.text: The wound still ached. One day he poled to the other shore again; the dry-season river was strangely loud—the river was laughing, mocking this old man; the reflection in the water was like his own father: in those days he too had forced his father to let go. He came back and confessed to the old man, pouring out all he had never told anyone; as he spoke he felt that the listener was plainly the river itself.

The old man took his hand and led him to sit by the river: You have heard its mockery, but you have not yet heard everything—listen further! On the water rose the images of father, himself, the son; three generations flowed into one river; joy and sorrow, good and evil, ten thousand voices became one great song. And when his heart no longer seized any one of them, only a single word remained in the song: Om. The wound began to close; he no longer fought his fate.

A few days later the old man looked a long time into his eyes: I have been waiting for this moment. Now that it has come, I may go. He turned into the woods, his step peaceful, his face as if it shone. That night he listened to the river alone the whole night through; among ten thousand sounds, what he heard was no longer farewell, but perfection.
Farewell, my hut; farewell, my river; farewell, my friend.

Many years later an old monk came out of his way to the ferry—he had heard that a saintly ferryman lived by this river. The ferryman said: Perhaps you have sought too much, and so cannot find; seeking means having a goal, finding means freedom. In the moment they knew each other the old monk stood as if struck by lightning: this time, still, he had not known his friend. On the morning of parting the old monk asked a last question: Have you some creed that upholds your life?
Wisdom cannot be spoken. Knowledge can be taught; wisdom cannot.

Already leaving, he turned back: Tell me a little more; my road is often hard and dark. The ferryman smiled and said softly: Bend closer; kiss my forehead. In the instant the old monk bent, he saw a thousand forms arising and passing; and over it all lay a transparent smile—the very smile of the Blessed One, which he had gazed upon all his life. He wept, and bowed deeply to the ground.
